title: Talent Management
tagline: Plan, hire, grow and keep the people your strategy depends on: practical talent management for Pakistani organisations.
description:
Most organisations do not fail for lack of strategy. They fail because the right people are not in the right chairs at the right time: sales teams churn faster than they can be hired, new joiners quit before they are productive, ratings reward the loudest voice, and a single retirement leaves a plant without anyone who knows how it really runs.

This certification gives you a complete, practical talent toolkit. You will build a **workforce plan** and a hiring funnel from real numbers, design **structured, competency-based interviews** that beat gut feel, run **onboarding** that keeps people, set **OKRs and KPIs**, run fair **calibration** and give feedback that changes behaviour. You will diagnose learning needs, apply **70-20-10** and **Kirkpatrick**, and calculate **training ROI**.

You will then map careers and potential on the **9-box grid**, plan **succession** for critical roles and reduce **key-person risk**, run **stay interviews**, cost turnover in PKR, use **total rewards**, compa-ratios and **inclusion** data, and turn HR numbers into **talent analytics** a board will act on.

Every stage is set in a Pakistani workplace, with calculations, judgement calls and games. Pass the final exam to earn your badge.
audience: HR business partners who advise managers on hiring, performance, development and retention
Line managers and department heads who recruit, rate, coach and keep their own teams
Talent acquisition, learning and development, and talent management leads
HR generalists moving into strategic or business-partnering roles
Founders and general managers of growing companies who own the people agenda
outcomes: Build a workforce plan that turns business targets, attrition and funnel yields into a realistic hiring and capability plan
Design structured, competency-based selection with anchored scoring and recognise the errors that distort hiring decisions
Run onboarding and performance management (OKRs, KPIs, calibration, SBI feedback) that is fair and keeps good people
Diagnose learning needs, apply 70-20-10, evaluate programmes with Kirkpatrick and calculate training ROI credibly
Use career paths, the 9-box grid and succession plans to grow high-potential talent and reduce key-person risk
Cost turnover, run stay interviews, apply total rewards and inclusion practices, and present talent analytics to leadership

quest.name: The Empty Chairs
quest.premise: Noor Valley Foods, a fast-growing Lahore food company, is losing people faster than it can hire them. Sales officers quit within months, a rival is circling its best area managers, and the plant head who keeps the Sundar factory running retires next year with no successor. Chief People Officer Farzana Qureshi brings you in as Talent Lead. Fill the empty chairs across five stages, then face the final boss: the board's talent review.

badge.name: Chair Keeper
badge.description: Awarded to talent professionals who can plan, hire, grow and keep the people an organisation's strategy depends on.

sessions.title: Workforce Planning, Employer Branding and Talent Acquisition
sessions.summary: Noor Valley needs 50 more sales officers and keeps losing the ones it has. Learn to turn strategy into a workforce plan, size the hiring funnel, sharpen the employer brand and replace gut-feel interviews with structured, competency-based selection.
objectives: Run the workforce planning cycle from business strategy to demand, supply, gap and action
Calculate hiring needs, attrition rates and funnel volumes from real numbers
Use the build, buy, borrow, bind and bounce options to close talent gaps
Design a structured, competency-based interview with anchored scoring and spot common selection errors

cards.title: Day one: the bucket with holes
cards.setting: Noor Valley Foods head office, Gulberg III, Lahore. Monday, 9:10 am.

lines.text: Your access card has not even been activated when Farzana Qureshi waves you into her office.
Welcome, Talent Lead. Good news first: the board approved our expansion into Sukkur and Hyderabad. Sales wants 50 more territory sales officers by December.
Bilal, National Sales. We have 180 TSOs today. I need 230. Just give me bodies, and I can spot a good salesman in five minutes.
Zoya, talent acquisition. Careful. Last year we lost about 30% of our TSOs. If that repeats, 50 hires won't even get us to 230.
Then hire faster! Every empty territory costs me shelf space to our competitors.
We are pouring water into a leaking bucket. Before we hire anyone, I want a real plan.
So, your first mission: how many people do we actually need to hire, and how do we pick the ones who will stay and sell?

scenes.heading: Start with the business
scenes.narration: Workforce planning always starts with strategy. Which markets, products and targets will the business chase? People needs follow from that, never the other way round.

scenes.heading: Forecast demand
scenes.narration: Next, estimate how many people, with which skills, the plan needs. Use ratios, trends, scenarios and the judgement of managers who know the work.

scenes.heading: Forecast supply
scenes.narration: Then look at what you will actually have: today's headcount minus expected leavers, retirements and transfers, plus people you can grow internally.

scenes.heading: Find the gap
scenes.narration: Demand minus supply is your gap. It can be a shortage, a surplus, or the right number of people with the wrong skills.

scenes.heading: Choose the actions
scenes.narration: Close the gap by building, buying, borrowing, binding or bouncing talent. Building suits long lead times and scarce markets, buying is faster but costs more, and borrowing fits temporary needs. Then monitor and update the plan.

cards.title: The workforce planning cycle
cards.caption: Plans are reviewed at least yearly and whenever strategy, budgets or the labour market shift.

items.label: Business strategy
items.detail: Targets, markets, products, budget and timelines set the direction.

items.label: Demand forecast
items.detail: Headcount and skills the plan needs, by role, location and date.

items.label: Supply forecast
items.detail: Current people minus expected exits, plus internal moves and promotions.

items.label: Gap analysis
items.detail: Shortages, surpluses and skill mismatches by role and timing.

items.label: Action plan
items.detail: Build, buy, borrow, bind or bounce, with owners, costs and dates.

items.label: Monitor and adjust
items.detail: Track hires, exits and productivity; refresh the plan when things change.

cards.title: Forecasting methods that actually work
cards.body:
**Demand** (what the plan needs):
- **Ratio or trend analysis**: use stable relationships, such as one TSO per 220 active outlets, or past growth. Works when the future looks like the past.
- **Scenario planning**: model best, expected and worst cases (for example, Sukkur launch on time or delayed). Best when uncertainty is high or there is no history.
- **Managerial judgement and Delphi**: experienced managers estimate needs; in a Delphi round, estimates are gathered anonymously and refined until they converge.

**Supply** (what you will have):
- Current headcount by role, grade and location.
- Expected leavers from attrition history, plus known retirements and contract ends.
- **Transition (Markov) analysis**: the share of people who typically stay, move up, move across or leave each year.
- The external labour market: how scarce the skill is in that city.

No method is perfect. Combine at least two and state your assumptions.

cards.title: Zoya's whiteboard: how many TSOs to hire?
cards.caption: A simple annual plan. Attrition is applied to today's headcount as a planning estimate.

items.label: TSOs today
items.detail: Current headcount across all regions.

items.label: TSOs needed by December
items.detail: Growth of 50 to staff Sukkur and Hyderabad.

items.label: Expected leavers
items.detail: 30% attrition applied to 180 people.

items.label: Hires required
items.detail: 50 for growth plus 54 to replace leavers.

cards.question: Using Zoya's method, a Faisalabad depot has 60 merchandisers, needs 75 by year end and expects 20% attrition on today's headcount. How many people must it hire?
cards.explanation: Growth is 75 minus 60, which is 15. Expected leavers are 20% of 60, which is 12. Hires required are 15 plus 12, so 27. Hiring only the growth number (15) ignores the people who will leave during the year.

cards.title: Five ways to close a talent gap
cards.prompt: Match each option to the Noor Valley move that illustrates it.

pairs.right: Train five strong merchandisers to become TSOs through a six-month academy.
Recruit experienced FMCG sales officers from the Hyderabad market.
Hire a contract team for six months to run the new ERP sales module rollout.
Give the only two SAP-trained planners a retention plan so they do not leave.
Exit roles made redundant when the old distributor billing system is closed.

cards.title: The five-minute hire
cards.setting: Sales floor, three weeks later. Bilal looks unusually quiet.

lines.text: Remember Hassan, the charming guy I hired for Sahiwal in one coffee? He left after six weeks. Half his visit logs were never made.
He is not the only one. Of the TSOs who left last year, a third went in their first 90 days. Most were hired after a single unstructured chat.
(on a WhatsApp call from Multan) The ones who stay know what this job is: 45 shops a day, heat, collections. Nobody tells candidates that.
So two problems. Our front door attracts the wrong people, and our interviews cannot tell the good from the merely confident.
Fix the brand, fix the funnel, then fix the interview. In that order.

cards.title: Employer brand, EVP and the realistic job preview
cards.body:
Your **employer brand** is what people *believe* it is like to work for you: shaped by ex-employees, WhatsApp groups, job sites and how you treat candidates.

Your **employee value proposition (EVP)** is what you deliberately *offer* in return for people's work: pay and benefits, career growth, work environment, culture and purpose. A strong EVP is:
- **True**: built from research with current staff, not wishful slogans.
- **Distinctive**: different from the rival hiring in the same city.
- **Targeted**: what matters to a TSO in Sukkur is not what matters to an analyst in Lahore.

An EVP that oversells creates a gap between promise and reality, and that gap shows up as early resignations.

The cure is a **realistic job preview (RJP)**: an honest picture of the job's hard parts (targets, travel, heat, cash collection) shared before the offer, through videos, ride-alongs or conversations with current staff. Some candidates self-select out, and those who join stay longer.

cards.title: The TSO hiring funnel
cards.caption: Work backwards from hires using each stage's yield (conversion rate) from past campaigns.

items.label: 2,600 applicants
items.detail: 50% pass the CV and phone screen.

items.label: 1,300 screened in
items.detail: 40% are invited to a structured interview.

items.label: 520 interviews
items.detail: 25% of interviewees receive an offer.

items.label: 130 offers
items.detail: 80% offer acceptance rate.

items.label: 104 hires
items.detail: The number the workforce plan requires.

cards.question: Noor Valley needs 20 Hyderabad hires. Offer acceptance is 80% and 25% of interviewees get an offer. How many candidates must be interviewed?
cards.explanation: Work backwards: offers needed are 20 divided by 0.8, which is 25. Interviews needed are 25 divided by 0.25, which is 100. Multiplying forwards instead of dividing backwards produces the wrong answers.

cards.title: Unstructured chat vs structured interview
cards.caption: Research on selection consistently finds structured interviews predict job performance better than unstructured ones.

items.label: Questions
items.left: Whatever comes to mind; different for each candidate
items.right: Same job-related questions for every candidate

items.label: Scoring
items.left: Overall gut feel at the end
items.right: Each answer rated on an anchored scale

items.label: Fairness
items.left: Easily swayed by bias and rapport

cards.title: Selection errors to catch in yourself

cards.back: One strong positive trait (a polished accent, a famous university) colours your rating of everything else.
The reverse of halo: one negative feature (a nervous start, a gap in the CV) drags every rating down.
Rating higher those who share your city, school, background or interests.
Forming a judgement in the first minutes and letting it override the evidence that follows.
Asking questions and noticing answers that support what you already believe about the candidate.
Rating a candidate relative to the one before: average looks great after a very weak interview.
Rating everyone high to be kind, or everyone in the middle to avoid committing.

cards.title: Which kind of interview question?
cards.prompt: Sort each question Zoya drafted for the TSO interview.

items.text: Tell me about a time a shopkeeper refused to stock your product. What did you do?
Describe the last time you missed a target. What happened and what did you change?
A retailer says a rival offers 5% more margin. What would you say to him?
If you had 45 shops to visit and your bike broke at noon, how would you plan the day?
Are you married, and do you plan to have children soon?
You are a hard worker, aren't you?
Give an example of collecting an overdue payment from a difficult customer.
Which sect do you belong to?

cards.title: The panel disagrees
cards.situation: You sit on a TSO interview panel with Bilal. Candidate Danish Raza is warm, confident and from Bilal's old college. His anchored scores on the four competencies average 2.1 out of 5, below the hiring bar of 3. Another candidate, Saima Baloch, was quieter but scored 3.8 with strong examples. Bilal says: 'Scores are paperwork. Danish will sell. Give him the Sukkur territory.' What do you do?

choices.text: Agree with Bilal: line managers own their hires and he knows sales.
choices.outcome: Danish joins and struggles with planning and collections, the competencies where he scored lowest. The structured process existed to prevent exactly this, and the panel has no defensible record for its decision.

choices.text: Walk through the evidence behind each score with Bilal and recommend Saima, noting the similar-to-me risk.
choices.outcome: Reviewing the specific answers shows Danish gave no examples for planning or collections. Bilal accepts that rapport and the shared college may have swayed him. Saima is hired and the decision is documented. Right approach: evidence over impression.

choices.text: Hire both to keep everyone happy.
choices.outcome: You avoid conflict, but you add a hire who did not meet the bar and use a second headcount the plan did not have. The real issue, overriding evidence with rapport, is left untouched.

choices.text: Reject both and restart the search so nobody can complain.
choices.outcome: Saima met the bar with strong evidence. Restarting wastes time, leaves the territory empty longer and punishes a good candidate for a disagreement about someone else.

cards.title: A competency question with an anchored scale
cards.body:
**Competency:** Customer persuasion. **Question:** 'Tell me about a time you convinced a reluctant retailer to take a new product.'

| Score | Anchor (what the answer shows) |
|---|---|
| 1 | No real example, or blames the retailer |
| 3 | Clear example; used price or scheme but little about the retailer's needs |
| 5 | Found the retailer's real concern (space, credit, slow sellers), tailored the offer, followed up, and can show the result |

The interviewer probes with the **STAR** structure: Situation, Task, Action (what *you* did, not 'we') and Result.

Each panel member scores **independently, before discussion**, citing the evidence. Only then do they compare and agree a final score. These **behaviourally anchored rating scales (BARS)** make scores consistent across interviewers and defensible if a decision is challenged.

cards.title: Build a structured interview
cards.prompt: Put Zoya's steps for designing the new TSO interview in the right order.
steps: Analyse the job: talk to top performers and managers about what success needs
Choose four or five critical competencies from that analysis
Write behavioural and situational questions for each competency
Write anchored rating scales describing weak, adequate and strong answers
Train the panel on the questions, scales and common rating errors
Interview, scoring each answer independently before the panel discusses
Track hires' later performance and retention to check the process works

cards.title: Assess well and measure the result
cards.body:
- **Mix methods.** Add a **work sample** (a role-played shop visit), a **situational judgement test** or an ability test to the interview.
- **Reliable vs valid.** A method is *reliable* if it gives consistent results; it is *valid* if those results actually predict job performance. You need both.
- **Measure the funnel.** **Time-to-fill** = days from approved vacancy to accepted offer. **Cost-per-hire** = total recruiting costs (ads, agency fees, recruiter time, assessments) ÷ hires.
- **Measure quality of hire.** The real test: new hires' performance and retention at 6 to 12 months.
- **Stay fair.** Never ask about marital plans, religion or sect.

cards.question: Two interviewers always give the same candidates almost identical scores, but a year later those scores show no link to how the hires actually perform. What is true of this interview?
options: It is valid but not reliable
It is both reliable and valid
It is reliable but not valid
It is neither, because the scores agree
cards.explanation: Consistent scores between raters show reliability. But if the scores do not predict performance, the method is not valid. A method can be reliable without being valid, though it cannot be valid if it is wildly unreliable.

cards.title: Stage one cleared: the bucket is mapped
items: Workforce planning runs from strategy to demand, supply, gap, action and review; combine at least two forecasting methods and state assumptions.
Hires required = growth + expected leavers; attrition rate = leavers ÷ average headcount × 100.
Size the funnel backwards: divide by each stage's yield, from accepted offers back to applicants.
Close gaps by building, buying, borrowing, binding or bouncing talent.
A true, targeted EVP and a realistic job preview attract people who stay.
Structured, competency-based interviews with anchored scales and independent scoring beat gut feel; watch for halo, similar-to-me, contrast and confirmation bias.

cards.prompt: Think of the last person your team hired. Which part of the decision rested on evidence of how they would do the job, and which on a feeling in the room? What one change from this stage would you make next time?

quiz.question: Farzana asks where Noor Valley's workforce planning should begin. What is the correct starting point?
options: The business strategy, targets and budget that the workforce must deliver
The number of CVs currently sitting in the recruitment inbox
Last year's headcount, increased by a standard 10% uplift for expected growth
A list of employees each manager would most like to replace
quiz.explanation: Workforce planning starts with the business strategy because people needs follow from markets, targets and budgets. Last year's headcount is an input to the supply forecast, not the starting point, and a flat uplift ignores what the business is actually planning.

quiz.question: A Hyderabad depot has 60 merchandisers and needs 75 by year end. It expects attrition of 20% on today's headcount. How many people must it hire?
quiz.explanation: Growth is 15 (75 minus 60) and expected leavers are 12 (20% of 60), so 27 hires are required. Hiring 15 covers only growth, so the depot would end the year short.

quiz.question: Noor Valley needs specialists for a six-month ERP rollout and will not need them afterwards. Which talent option fits best?
options: Build: put existing staff through a two-year development programme
Bind: offer retention bonuses to current ERP users
Borrow: bring in contractors or a consulting team for the project
Bounce: release staff whose roles the ERP may change
quiz.explanation: A temporary, time-bound need is best met by borrowing talent through contractors or consultants. Building takes too long for a six-month project, and binding retains people you already have rather than filling the gap.

quiz.question: A region started the year with 80 TSOs and ended with 100. During the year 27 TSOs left. What was its attrition rate?
quiz.explanation: Attrition rate = leavers ÷ average headcount × 100. Average headcount is (80 + 100) ÷ 2 = 90, so 27 ÷ 90 = 30%. Dividing by the closing headcount gives 27%, and dividing by the opening headcount gives 33.75%.

quiz.question: What is the difference between an employer brand and an employee value proposition (EVP)?
options: The brand covers pay and benefits only, while the EVP covers only the softer side of working life: culture, values and purpose
The brand is how people see you as an employer; the EVP is the offer you deliberately make in return for work
The brand is set by the marketing team; the EVP is set by the finance team
They are two names for the same recruitment advertising budget
quiz.explanation: The employer brand is the reputation or perception of the employer, shaped by many voices. The EVP is the deliberate offer (pay, growth, environment, culture, purpose) the organisation makes. Both cover more than pay.

quiz.question: Which feature most clearly makes an interview 'structured'?
options: Every candidate is asked the same job-related questions and each answer is rated on an anchored scale
The interview is held in a formal boardroom with at least four senior panel members who each ask their own favourite questions
The interviewer follows the conversation wherever the candidate's answers lead
The candidate is asked to describe their strengths and weaknesses
quiz.explanation: Structure means consistent, job-related questions derived from the job analysis and answers rated against anchored scales. A formal room or large panel does not make an interview structured, and following the conversation freely is the hallmark of an unstructured chat.

quiz.question: An interviewer is impressed that a candidate studied at a well-known Lahore business school and rates him highly on planning, persuasion and integrity, although he gave weak examples for each. Which error is this?
options: Contrast effect
Central tendency
Halo effect
Horns effect
quiz.explanation: One positive feature (the school) is colouring the ratings of unrelated competencies, which is the halo effect. The horns effect is the negative version, and the contrast effect depends on comparison with a previous candidate.

quiz.question: Which of these is a behavioural interview question rather than a situational one?
options: What would you do if a shopkeeper refused to pay an overdue amount?
How would you handle a retailer who wants a bigger discount?
If your route had 50 shops and you only had time for 40 of them, what would you do?
Tell me about a time you recovered an overdue payment from a difficult shopkeeper
quiz.explanation: Behavioural questions ask about past behaviour ('tell me about a time'). The others describe hypothetical situations ('what would you do'), which makes them situational questions. Both types are useful in a structured interview.

quiz.question: You need 20 hires. Past campaigns show 80% of offers are accepted and 25% of interviewees receive offers. How many candidates should you plan to interview?
quiz.explanation: Offers needed = 20 ÷ 0.8 = 25. Interviews needed = 25 ÷ 0.25 = 100. Working forwards by multiplying (for example 20 × 0.8 × ...) understates the volume because each stage loses candidates.

quiz.question: Zoya finds that two panel members give almost identical scores to the same candidates, but the scores show no relationship with the hires' sales performance a year later. What should she conclude?
options: The interview is valid because the two raters agree with each other
The interview is unreliable, so both raters need refresher training on using the anchored rating scale consistently
The interview is working and the hires' managers are rating them unfairly
It is reliable but not valid, so the questions and competencies need redesigning
quiz.explanation: Agreement between raters shows reliability. Validity means scores predict job performance, which these do not. The fix is to revisit the job analysis and questions, not to retrain raters who are already consistent.

sessions.title: Onboarding for Retention and Performance Management
sessions.summary: The new hires are arriving, and some are already walking out. Design onboarding that keeps people and speeds them to full productivity, then fix a performance system where everyone 'exceeds' but targets are missed: OKRs, KPIs, calibration, rating biases and feedback that works.
objectives: Design onboarding around compliance, clarification, culture and connection, from preboarding to day 90
Calculate early attrition and the cost of slow ramp-up
Write KPIs and OKRs correctly and score key results
Run a calibration session that reduces rating bias and give SBI feedback that changes behaviour

cards.title: Nine chairs empty again
cards.setting: People team huddle room, Lahore. Three months into the hiring drive.

lines.text: Bad news. We hired 40 TSOs with the new interviews. Nine have already left, all within 90 days.
So your fancy interviews don't work either!
The exit calls say otherwise. No phone or tablet for two weeks. No route plan. One man in Sukkur never met his manager until week five.
(joining from Multan) I gave my two new joiners a buddy and rode with them in the first week. Both are still here.
Selection got the right people through the door. Onboarding decided whether they stayed.
And there is a second fire. Year-end ratings are due, and Bilal's region has rated 70% of TSOs 'exceeds' while missing target.
My people work hard. What am I supposed to do, punish them?
Your mission: fix the first 90 days, then fix how we set goals and judge performance.

scenes.heading: It starts before day one
scenes.narration: Preboarding is the time between offer and start date. A welcome call, a clear joining plan and paperwork done early stop new hires from accepting a rival's last-minute offer.

scenes.heading: Compliance
scenes.narration: The basics: contract, policies, CNIC copies, bank account, EOBI and social security registration, safety rules. Necessary, but never the whole programme.

scenes.heading: Clarification
scenes.narration: Making the job clear: targets, routes, tools, who to ask. People who know exactly what good looks like ramp up faster.

scenes.heading: Culture
scenes.narration: How things really work here: values, norms, unwritten rules and the stories that explain them.

scenes.heading: Connection
scenes.narration: Relationships: a buddy, regular one-to-ones with the manager, introductions to key colleagues. Connection is the strongest early protection against quitting.

cards.title: Which C is this?
cards.prompt: Match each onboarding activity to the part of onboarding it mainly serves.

pairs.right: Signing the code of conduct and completing harassment-policy and safety briefings
A written 30-60-90 day plan with outlet targets and the route map
The regional head tells stories of how the company handled a product recall honestly
A buddy from a nearby territory rides along for the first week
A welcome call and a joining kit sent the week before the start date

cards.question: Of 48 new hires in Hyderabad, 12 left within their first 90 days. What is the 90-day attrition rate?
cards.explanation: Early (90-day) attrition = leavers in the first 90 days ÷ new hires × 100 = 12 ÷ 48 = 25%. Dividing by the depot's whole headcount would hide how badly onboarding is doing.

cards.title: KPIs, OKRs and SMART goals
cards.body:
**KPIs (key performance indicators)** measure the ongoing health of a job or business: outlets visited per day, collection days, numeric distribution. They are tracked continuously and have targets.

**OKRs (objectives and key results)** drive change or a push for a period, usually a quarter:
- **Objective**: qualitative, inspiring, short. 'Make Noor Valley the first choice for Sukkur retailers.'
- **Key results**: usually 2 to 5, measurable outcomes (not activities). 'Increase active outlets in Sukkur from 400 to 650.'
- Key results are often scored 0.0 to 1.0 and averaged. For stretch OKRs many companies treat about 0.6 to 0.7 as healthy; always hitting 1.0 suggests goals were not ambitious.

**SMART** goals are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

Use **leading indicators** (calls made, new outlets opened) to steer and **lagging indicators** (sales, market share) to judge results.

cards.title: KPI or OKR?
cards.caption: Most roles need both: KPIs keep the engine healthy, OKRs move it somewhere new.

items.label: Purpose
items.right: Drive a specific change or stretch

items.label: Form
items.right: Qualitative objective plus 2 to 5 measurable results

items.label: Ambition
items.right: Stretch; partial achievement can be a success

items.label: Example
items.left: Average collection period of 21 days or less
items.right: Grow Sukkur active outlets from 400 to 650

cards.question: Rubina's quarterly OKR has three key results scored 0.7, 0.5 and 0.9. What is the OKR's score, and how would many OKR users read it for a stretch goal?
options: 0.5: a failure, because the lowest result counts
0.9: excellent, because the best result counts
2.1: well above target
0.7: a healthy result for a stretch goal
cards.explanation: OKR scores are usually the average of the key results: (0.7 + 0.5 + 0.9) ÷ 3 = 0.7. For stretch goals, around 0.6 to 0.7 is often treated as healthy. The score is not the lowest, highest or total.

cards.title: The calibration room
cards.setting: Boardroom, Lahore. Regional sales managers dial in for year-end calibration.

lines.text: We compare ratings across regions today. Bilal, your region has 70% 'exceeds' and is at 88% of target.
My people try hard! And the Sukkur team had a very good December.
December was strong, yes. But January to October, Sukkur was the weakest territory in the country.
And Rubina only gets 'meets'. She argues with me in every meeting. Attitude matters.
(quietly, on the call) I delivered 128% of target and opened 140 new outlets. I argued about the scheme because it was losing us money.
Then let's look at the evidence for everyone, against the same standard.

cards.title: Rating biases in the calibration room

cards.back: Rating everyone generously, often to avoid conflict or protect the team's bonus.
Rating everyone harshly, so nobody 'exceeds' even when they should.
Putting almost everyone in the middle to avoid hard conversations.
Letting the last month or two outweigh the whole review period.
One trait, good or bad (like disagreeing with the boss), colours every other rating.
Requiring fixed shares of people in each rating band. It can curb leniency, but in small or uniformly strong teams it forces unfair labels and damages trust.
Ratings often reveal more about the rater's own tendencies than about the person rated. Multiple raters and calibration reduce it.

cards.title: Running a fair calibration session
cards.caption: Calibration aligns standards across managers; it is not a negotiation about budgets.

items.label: Prepare data
items.detail: Ratings, results versus target, and the rating spread per manager.

items.label: Restate the standard
items.detail: What 'meets' and 'exceeds' mean, with examples.

items.label: Review outliers
items.detail: Start with unusual ratings and managers with skewed spreads.

items.label: Ask for evidence
items.detail: Specific results and behaviours over the whole period.

items.label: Challenge bias
items.detail: Name leniency, recency, halo or similar-to-me when you see it.

items.label: Record decisions
items.detail: Note changes and reasons; managers explain final ratings.

cards.title: Bilal versus the evidence
cards.situation: In calibration, Bilal insists Rubina stays at 'meets' because of her 'attitude'. Her results are the strongest in the region. Noor Valley's framework rates both results and values-based behaviours, and 'challenges respectfully with data' is listed as a positive behaviour. As facilitator, what do you do?

choices.text: Ask Bilal for specific examples of behaviour that broke the framework, review them against her results and the framework, and decide on that evidence.
choices.outcome: Bilal's examples are all about Rubina disagreeing with the scheme in meetings, with data, which the framework rewards. The panel rates her 'exceeds' and records why. Right approach: evidence against a shared standard, with the bias named.

choices.text: Accept Bilal's rating; he is her manager and sees her every day.
choices.outcome: Manager authority does not remove bias. Rubina's strongest-in-region results are ignored and she learns that disagreeing is punished. Calibration exists precisely to catch this.

choices.text: Raise Rubina to 'exceeds' without discussion, since the numbers speak for themselves.
choices.outcome: The outcome may be right, but skipping the discussion leaves Bilal unconvinced and leaves the behaviour question untested. Calibration should test evidence, not overrule managers silently.

choices.text: Put everyone in Bilal's region at 'meets' so nobody is treated unfairly.
choices.outcome: Flattening ratings is central tendency imposed from the top. It erases real differences and demotivates the best performers.

cards.title: Performance as a cycle, not an annual event
cards.caption: Year-end ratings should hold no surprises if the cycle runs all year.

items.label: Plan
items.detail: Agree KPIs, OKRs and behaviours at the start.

items.label: Check in
items.detail: Monthly one-to-ones on progress and blockers.

items.label: Feedback
items.detail: Specific, timely feedback, both positive and corrective.

items.label: Review
items.detail: Mid-year and year-end assessment against evidence.

items.label: Develop
items.detail: Agree development actions, then reset goals.

cards.title: The SBI feedback model
cards.body:
Vague feedback ('you need to be more professional') makes people defensive because they cannot act on it. **SBI** keeps feedback specific and fair:

- **Situation**: when and where. 'At Tuesday's distributor meeting in Sukkur...'
- **Behaviour**: what you saw or heard, observable and factual, with no labels about character. '...you checked your phone while the distributor explained his stock problem...'
- **Impact**: the effect on you, the customer or the result. '...he told me afterwards he felt we didn't care, and he delayed his order.'

Then **pause and listen**, and agree what happens next. SBI works for praise too.

**Avoid the 'feedback sandwich'** (praise, criticism, praise): people learn to discount the praise or miss the message.

**Feedforward** adds a future focus: 'Next time, what could you do differently?' It helps people own the change.

cards.title: An SBI conversation, step by step
cards.prompt: Put the steps of Bilal's feedback conversation with a TSO in order.
steps: Choose a private moment soon after the event
Describe the situation: when and where it happened
Describe the specific, observable behaviour
Explain the impact on the customer, team or result
Pause and ask for the TSO's view
Agree together what will happen next time and when you will follow up

cards.question: Which statement is a 'behaviour' in SBI terms?
options: 'You arrived 40 minutes after the store manager and the meeting had started.'
'You are careless about time.'
'You don't respect our customers.'
'You have a bad attitude about punctuality.'
cards.explanation: SBI behaviours are observable facts that a camera could record. The other options are labels or judgements about character, which cause defensiveness and give the person nothing specific to change.

cards.title: Underperformance vs misconduct
cards.body:
- **Capability** (cannot yet meet the standard) and **misconduct** (breaks rules, for example falsified visit logs) are different problems with different processes.
- For capability, use a **performance improvement plan (PIP)**: specific, measurable standards, support offered, a fair timeline, documented reviews.
- For misconduct, follow your disciplinary procedure: typically a written show-cause notice, a chance to reply and an inquiry where required, before any penalty. Pakistan's standing orders laws (now provincial) set rules for workmen; check the current law and your policy.
- Never use a PIP as a disguised exit or skip due process because 'everyone knows'.

cards.title: SBI in Bilal's own words
cards.body:
Bilal practises on a TSO, Kashif, whose Hyderabad shops keep running out of stock.

**Before:** 'Kashif, you're lazy with orders. Fix it.' Kashif shuts down.

**After:** 'Kashif, on last week's route (**situation**), four of your top ten shops placed no reorder because their stock was not checked during the visit (**behaviour**). Two of them filled the shelf with a rival's ketchup, and we lost about PKR 60,000 in sales (**impact**). What happened on those visits?'

Kashif explains the new handheld app crashes in low signal areas, so he skipped the stock count. They agree he will use the paper backup sheet and Bilal will log the app fault with IT. A follow-up is set for next Monday.

The specific version found a **system problem** that the label 'lazy' would have hidden.

cards.title: Stage two cleared: the door holds
items: Onboarding spans preboarding to day 90 and covers compliance, clarification, culture and connection; connection is the strongest early retention lever.
90-day attrition = leavers within 90 days ÷ new hires; ramp-up gap = months × full output × shortfall.
KPIs monitor ongoing health; OKRs drive change with a qualitative objective and 2 to 5 measurable key results, scored and averaged.
Calibration compares ratings against one standard with evidence and names biases such as leniency, recency and halo.
Give SBI feedback: situation, observable behaviour, impact, then listen and agree next steps.
Handle capability with a fair PIP and misconduct with due disciplinary process; never mix them up.

cards.prompt: Recall the last piece of critical feedback you gave or received. Rewrite it in SBI form. What changes in how it would land and in what the person could actually do with it?

quiz.question: A new TSO in Sukkur is paired with an experienced colleague from the next territory, who rides with him in week one and calls him daily in week two. Which part of onboarding does this mainly serve?
options: Compliance
Clarification
Connection
Culture
quiz.explanation: A buddy builds relationships and support, which is connection. Clarification is about making the job's targets, tools and expectations clear; compliance covers contracts, policies and registrations.

quiz.question: Noor Valley hired 60 TSOs this year. Fifteen left within 90 days and another 6 left later in the year. What was the 90-day attrition rate?
quiz.explanation: 90-day attrition = 15 ÷ 60 = 25%. The later 6 leavers are not early attrition; adding them (21 ÷ 60) gives 35%, which answers a different question.

quiz.question: Why does preboarding matter between an accepted offer and the first day?
options: It gives the company time to renegotiate the salary downwards if a cheaper candidate appears before the start date
It replaces the need for a 90-day review
It keeps the new hire engaged and ready, reducing last-minute drop-outs and making day one productive
It is where the employment contract is first negotiated
quiz.explanation: Preboarding (welcome call, documents, devices, a clear joining plan) keeps the new hire committed and ready, which reduces drop-outs to counter-offers. It does not replace later onboarding or the 90-day review.

quiz.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a KPI from an OKR?
options: A KPI is a qualitative statement of intent, while an OKR is always a single financial number reviewed by the finance team every month
A KPI is set once a year; an OKR never has numbers
A KPI applies to managers; an OKR applies only to frontline staff
A KPI tracks ongoing performance against a target; an OKR pairs a qualitative objective with measurable results to drive change
quiz.explanation: KPIs track ongoing health and are expected to be met. OKRs pair an inspiring qualitative objective with 2 to 5 measurable key results for a period such as a quarter, often as a stretch.

quiz.question: An OKR has four key results scored 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0. What is the OKR's score?
quiz.explanation: Average the key results: (0.4 + 0.6 + 0.8 + 1.0) ÷ 4 = 2.8 ÷ 4 = 0.7. Using the lowest, highest or the sum misreads how OKRs are usually scored.

quiz.question: A regional manager rates 22 of his 24 people 'meets expectations', including his best and weakest performers, saying he 'does not want drama'. Which rating bias is this?
options: Recency
Central tendency
Severity
Similar-to-me bias
quiz.explanation: Clustering almost everyone in the middle to avoid hard conversations is central tendency. Severity would push ratings down, and recency is about over-weighting the latest events.

quiz.question: A TSO struggled from January to October but had an outstanding November and December. Her manager rates her 'exceeds' for the year. What bias is most likely?
options: Leniency
Recency
Contrast
Similar-to-me
quiz.explanation: Letting the last two months outweigh the whole review period is recency bias. Leniency is generous rating across the board, not weighting by time.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of a calibration session?
options: To reduce the bonus budget by lowering ratings across the board until the cost fits what finance has approved
To let senior leaders change ratings without explaining why
To replace managers' ratings with HR's own assessment
To apply one consistent rating standard across managers using evidence, reducing individual rater bias
quiz.explanation: Calibration aligns standards across raters and tests ratings against evidence. It is not a budget-cutting exercise, and decisions should be recorded and explained, not imposed silently.

quiz.question: Which feedback follows the SBI model?
options: 'In this morning's meeting you interrupted Mr Soomro three times as he explained his credit issue, and he left without confirming the order.'
'You are rude to distributors and need to change your attitude.'
'You're doing a great job generally, but you could be a bit better with distributors sometimes, though overall you're absolutely fine and I'm happy.'
'Everyone says you have problems with people, so please work on it.'
quiz.explanation: The first option gives the situation (this morning's meeting), the observable behaviour (interrupted three times) and the impact (no confirmed order). The others are labels, a vague sandwich or hearsay.

quiz.question: A TSO has missed target for two quarters. During the review, the manager also finds that he recorded shop visits he never made. How should the two issues be handled?
options: Put both issues into a single PIP, since missed targets and false visit records are both simply performance problems to coach
Dismiss him immediately for missing targets, since the false records prove he is not trying
Handle missed targets through a PIP and the false records through the disciplinary procedure, with due process
Ignore the false records if his sales improve within the PIP period
quiz.explanation: Capability and misconduct need different processes. Missed targets call for a PIP with support and a fair timeline; falsified records are misconduct, handled through the disciplinary procedure (show-cause, a chance to reply, an inquiry where required). Merging them or skipping due process is unfair and risky.

sessions.title: Learning and Development That Pays Back
sessions.summary: The CFO wants to cut the learning budget and Bilal wants a three-day sales course for everyone. Diagnose real learning needs, design with 70-20-10, evaluate with Kirkpatrick's four levels and calculate training ROI that a finance team will believe.
objectives: Run a training needs analysis at organisation, job and individual level and spot problems training cannot fix
Design development using the 70-20-10 guideline
Evaluate programmes at Kirkpatrick's four levels and add ROI as a fifth
Calculate fully loaded costs, isolate a programme's effect, and work out ROI and the benefit-cost ratio

cards.title: The budget axe
cards.setting: Farzana's office, Lahore. A printout of the training budget, covered in red ink.

lines.text: The CFO wants to cut learning by 40%. His words: 'Training is a holiday with lunch. Show me what it returns.'
Cut it? I need more! Hyderabad sales fell 15% this quarter. Book a three-day sales course for all 230 TSOs.
(on the line from Sundar) And my line supervisors need food-safety refreshers before the next audit. That one is not optional.
Before we book anything: do we know why Hyderabad fell? Last month's mystery shopper scores there were actually our best.
Exactly. We will spend on the right problems and prove what each programme returns.
Your mission: find the real needs, design learning that sticks, and measure it in rupees.

cards.title: Is it really a training problem?

scenes.heading: Start with the gap
scenes.narration: Training needs analysis starts with a performance gap: what people should achieve compared with what they achieve now.

scenes.heading: Organisation level
scenes.narration: First, look at the organisation: strategy, new products, regulations and results data show where capability matters most.

scenes.heading: Job level
scenes.narration: Next, analyse the job or task: which knowledge, skills and behaviours does the role need to perform to standard?

scenes.heading: Individual level
scenes.narration: Then look at individuals: who actually lacks those skills? Assessments, observations and appraisal data tell you.

scenes.heading: Rule out other causes
scenes.narration: Ask one question: could they do it if their life depended on it? If yes, the problem is tools, processes, incentives or clarity, and training will not fix it.

cards.title: Training needs analysis in practice
cards.caption: Training is only one answer; the analysis often points to a fix elsewhere.

items.label: Define the gap
items.detail: Desired versus current performance, in numbers.

items.label: Organisational analysis
items.detail: Strategy, results and risks show where skills matter.

items.label: Job or task analysis
items.detail: Knowledge, skills and behaviours the role needs.

items.label: Individual analysis
items.detail: Who lacks them, from assessments and observation.

items.label: Find root causes
items.detail: Separate skill gaps from tool, process or incentive problems.

items.label: Choose solutions
items.detail: Learning where skills are missing; other fixes elsewhere.

cards.title: Can training fix it?
cards.prompt: Zoya's Hyderabad investigation found these causes. Sort each one.

items.text: New TSOs cannot explain the margin benefits of the new sauce range
The incentive scheme pays more for old SKUs than the new range
Handheld order app crashes in low-signal areas
Supervisors do not know how to coach on a ride-along
Distributor's van visits each shop only every ten days
Experienced TSOs know the pitch but no one checks visit quality
Line workers have not learned the new allergen-handling procedure
Targets for Hyderabad were set before a rival halved its prices

cards.question: Experienced Hyderabad TSOs scored highly on a product knowledge test and a role-play, yet sales of the new range are falling. The incentive scheme pays more for old products. What does the needs analysis suggest?
options: Run a three-day product course for all TSOs
Fix the incentive scheme; skills are not the main gap
Test the TSOs again with a harder exam
Replace the experienced TSOs with new hires
cards.explanation: The TSOs can do the job well when tested, so this is not a skill gap. They are responding to incentives that reward old products. Training would cost money without changing behaviour.

cards.title: The 70-20-10 guideline
cards.body:
**70-20-10** describes how people, especially managers, report learning most of what made them effective:

- **About 70% from experience**: stretch assignments, new projects, rotations, solving real problems.
- **About 20% from others**: coaching, mentoring, feedback, buddies, peer networks.
- **About 10% from formal learning**: courses, e-learning, workshops, reading.

Use it as a **design guideline, not a formula or a budget rule**. The numbers came from studies of what successful executives recalled, so they are approximate.

The practical point: formal training works best when it is *connected* to experience and support. A two-day negotiation course (10) followed by negotiating real distributor contracts (70) with a manager debrief after each (20) beats the course alone.

The common mistake is using 70-20-10 as an excuse to cut all formal learning. The model never said formal learning does not matter.

cards.title: Sort Rubina's development plan
cards.prompt: Rubina is being developed for a regional role. Sort each activity into the 70-20-10 guideline.

items.text: Leads the Sukkur launch task force for six months
Monthly mentoring sessions with the Head of Sales of another division
Completes an online course in sales finance
Covers for the regional manager during his Hajj leave
Gets 360-degree feedback and debriefs it with a coach
Attends a two-day negotiation workshop in Lahore
Renegotiates the Multan distributor contract herself
Joins a peer network of area managers that meets online every fortnight

cards.title: Show me the money
cards.setting: Finance floor. The CFO's assistant forwards a WhatsApp voice note.

lines.text: Voice note from the CFO: 'Happy sheets saying people enjoyed lunch do not count. What changed in the business?'
Easy. After last year's negotiation course, Sukkur margins went up 20%. Training did that.
Prices also rose and a rival distributor closed in Sukkur that same quarter. Some of that 20% would have come anyway.
So how do we prove anything?
We evaluate at every level, isolate what the programme caused, and turn it into rupees, honestly.
Overclaim once and the CFO will never believe us again.

cards.title: Kirkpatrick's four levels, plus ROI
cards.caption: Higher levels are harder to measure but matter more to the business. Each level builds on the ones below.

items.label: Level 5: ROI
items.detail: Phillips' addition: net monetary benefit compared with fully loaded cost.

items.label: Level 4: Results
items.detail: Business outcomes: sales, margin, errors, safety incidents, retention.

items.label: Level 3: Behaviour
items.detail: Are people applying it on the job weeks or months later?

items.label: Level 2: Learning
items.detail: Did knowledge or skill improve? Tests, role-plays, demonstrations.

items.label: Level 1: Reaction
items.detail: Did participants find it relevant, engaging and useful?

cards.title: Which level is this evidence?
cards.prompt: Match each piece of evaluation evidence to its level.

pairs.right: Participants rate the coaching workshop 4.6 out of 5 for relevance
Supervisors' scores on a coaching role-play rise from 52% to 81%
Ride-along audits show supervisors coaching on 70% of visits after three months
Coached territories grow sales 6% faster than uncoached ones
Net benefits of PKR 4.2m on fully loaded costs of PKR 3m

cards.question: Learning scores after a coaching course are excellent, but three months later ride-along audits show supervisors are not coaching. Managers never discussed the course with them. Where is the problem most likely?
options: The participants' reaction (Level 1)
The course content, since learning scores are high
Transfer to the job (Level 3), driven by a lack of manager support
Business results (Level 4), so the course should be dropped
cards.explanation: Strong Level 2 with weak Level 3 points to a transfer problem: people learned but are not applying it. Manager support before and after training is one of the strongest drivers of transfer.

cards.title: Training ROI the CFO will trust
cards.body:
**Benefit-cost ratio (BCR)** = programme benefits ÷ programme costs.

**ROI (%)** = (programme benefits − programme costs) ÷ programme costs × 100. So a BCR of 2.4 equals an ROI of 140%.

To make the numbers credible:
- **Fully load the costs**: needs analysis and design, facilitators, venue, materials, travel, evaluation, and **participants' salary for time away from work**.
- **Isolate the programme's effect**: use a **control group** (similar people who did not attend), **trend analysis**, or participant and manager **estimates** of how much of the improvement the programme caused, multiplied by their confidence in that estimate.
- **Convert to money** using standard values: margin, cost of an error, cost of a leaver.
- **Be conservative**: for short programmes, count only first-year benefits.
- Report **intangibles** (morale, teamwork) separately when they cannot be credibly converted.

cards.title: ROI of the Multan coaching pilot
cards.caption: All costs fully loaded, and benefits isolated to the programme's effect.

items.label: Fully loaded costs
items.detail: Design, delivery, travel, evaluation and participants' time.

items.label: Isolated benefits
items.detail: Extra first-year margin attributed to the programme.

items.label: Net benefits
items.detail: PKR 9.6m minus PKR 4.0m.

items.label: ROI
items.detail: Net benefits ÷ costs × 100.

items.label: Benefit-cost ratio
items.detail: Benefits ÷ costs: PKR 2.40 back per rupee spent.

cards.question: A programme costs PKR 1.5m fully loaded and produces isolated benefits of PKR 2.4m. What are its ROI and BCR?
options: ROI 60%, BCR 1.6
ROI 160%, BCR 1.6
ROI 60%, BCR 0.6
ROI 90%, BCR 1.9
cards.explanation: Net benefits = 2.4 − 1.5 = PKR 0.9m, so ROI = 0.9 ÷ 1.5 = 60%. BCR = 2.4 ÷ 1.5 = 1.6. A common error is to quote the BCR as if it were the ROI percentage (160%).

cards.title: Isolating the effect: Zoya's estimate method
cards.body:
After a negotiation programme, participating TSOs' annual margin improved by **PKR 10m** compared with the year before. Prices and a rival's exit also helped, and no control group existed.

Zoya asks each participant's manager: 'What share of this improvement came from the programme, and how confident are you in that estimate?' The average answer is **60%** attributed, with **75%** confidence.

**Isolated benefit** = 10m × 60% × 75% = **PKR 4.5m**.

Fully loaded costs were **PKR 2.5m**, including TSOs' salaries for two days away from their routes.

- Net benefit = 4.5 − 2.5 = PKR 2.0m
- **ROI** = 2.0 ÷ 2.5 = **80%**
- **BCR** = 4.5 ÷ 2.5 = **1.8**

The confidence adjustment makes the figure conservative, and the CFO can see every assumption. Where possible, a control group (for example, a similar region that trains later) gives stronger evidence than estimates.

cards.title: Bilal's 20%
cards.situation: Bilal wants to tell the board: 'Our negotiation course raised Sukkur margins by 20%, so its ROI is enormous.' You know prices rose and a rival distributor closed in the same quarter. A similar region, Hyderabad, has not yet taken the course. The board meets in two weeks. What do you recommend?

choices.text: Present the full 20% as the course's result; it is the board's job to ask questions.
choices.outcome: A finance director spots the price rise in minutes. The whole L&D case loses credibility, and next year's budget is cut harder. Overclaiming is the fastest way to lose a CFO.

choices.text: Compare Sukkur with Hyderabad as a control group, adjust for the price rise, and present the isolated, fully loaded ROI with assumptions shown.
choices.outcome: Hyderabad's margins rose 12% with the price rise and no course, so only about 8 points of Sukkur's gain is left to explain, and part of that came from the rival's exit. The conservative ROI is smaller but still positive, and the board trusts it. Right approach: isolate, then convert.

choices.text: Present only participants' satisfaction scores, since ROI is too hard to prove.
choices.outcome: Reaction data does not answer the CFO's question about business change. It confirms his view that training cannot show results.

choices.text: Present the 20% but add a footnote that other factors may have contributed.
choices.outcome: More honest than the first option, but the headline is still overstated and the footnote invites doubt. With a control group available, you can do much better.

cards.title: Run an ROI evaluation
cards.prompt: Put the steps of an ROI study in order.
steps: Agree the business measures and evaluation plan before the programme starts
Collect reaction and learning data during and at the end of the programme
Collect behaviour and business-results data after people are back at work
Isolate the programme's effect from other factors
Convert the isolated results into monetary values
Tally fully loaded costs and calculate ROI and BCR
Report results with assumptions and intangible benefits

cards.title: Make learning stick
cards.body:
- **Forgetting is fast.** Without reinforcement, people forget much of new learning within days or weeks. Plan for it.
- **Space and retrieve.** Short follow-up quizzes, practice and refreshers spaced over weeks beat one long session.
- **Involve the manager.** A conversation before training ('what do you want from it?') and after ('what will you apply first?') drives transfer more than almost anything in the classroom.
- **Apply it fast.** Give a real task to use the skill within days.
- **Evaluate beyond happy sheets.** Plan Level 3 and 4 measures before the programme starts, not after.

cards.title: Stage three cleared: the budget survives
items: Training needs analysis works at organisation, job and individual level; rule out tools, processes and incentives before prescribing training.
70-20-10 is a design guideline: connect formal learning to experience and support; never use it as an excuse to drop formal learning.
Kirkpatrick: reaction, learning, behaviour, results; ROI is Phillips' fifth level. Strong learning with weak behaviour points to a transfer problem.
ROI = (benefits − costs) ÷ costs × 100; BCR = benefits ÷ costs. A BCR of 2.4 is an ROI of 140%.
Fully load costs (including participants' time), isolate effects with control groups, trends or confidence-adjusted estimates, and report intangibles separately.

cards.prompt: Pick one training programme your organisation ran last year. At which Kirkpatrick level was it evaluated? What would you need to collect, and from whom, to show its effect at Level 4?

quiz.question: Which level of training needs analysis asks which knowledge, skills and behaviours a role requires to perform to standard?
options: Organisational analysis
Individual analysis
Reaction analysis
Job or task analysis
quiz.explanation: Job (task) analysis defines what the role requires. Organisational analysis looks at strategy and where capability matters most, and individual analysis identifies who lacks the required skills.

quiz.question: Packing-line operators at the Sundar factory know the new labelling procedure and can demonstrate it perfectly, but errors persist because the labelling machine jams and they skip the check to keep the line moving. What should Tariq do first?
options: Retrain every operator on the labelling procedure in a half-day refresher session
Fix the machine and the line-speed pressure, since this is not a skills gap
Introduce a written test on labelling for every shift
Add the procedure to the induction programme for new hires
quiz.explanation: Operators can do the task correctly, so training will not solve it. The causes are equipment and process pressure. Retraining or testing people who already know the procedure wastes money.

quiz.question: Rubina is asked to lead the Sukkur launch task force for six months as part of her development. Under the 70-20-10 guideline, this is:
options: Learning from others (the 20)
Formal learning (the 10)
Learning from experience (the 70)
Outside the model, since it is a business role
quiz.explanation: A stretch assignment on real work is learning from experience. Mentoring or coaching would be the 20, and courses or e-learning the 10.

quiz.question: Three months after a coaching course, ride-along audits check whether supervisors are actually coaching their TSOs. Which Kirkpatrick level is this?
options: Level 3: Behaviour
Level 1: Reaction
Level 2: Learning
Level 4: Results
quiz.explanation: Observing whether people apply the learning on the job is Level 3. Level 2 measures knowledge or skill gained during training, and Level 4 measures business outcomes such as sales.

quiz.question: A programme's fully loaded cost is PKR 2.0m and its isolated first-year benefits are PKR 5.0m. What is its ROI?
quiz.explanation: ROI = (5.0 − 2.0) ÷ 2.0 × 100 = 150%. The figure 250% is the benefit-cost ratio (2.5) expressed as a percentage, a common mistake.

quiz.question: A programme reports a benefit-cost ratio of 2.5 : 1. What ROI does this equal?
quiz.explanation: A BCR of 2.5 means PKR 2.50 of benefit per rupee of cost, so net benefit is PKR 1.50 per rupee: an ROI of 150%. ROI is always BCR minus one, expressed as a percentage.

quiz.question: Which method gives the strongest evidence that a programme, rather than other factors, caused an improvement?
options: Asking participants whether they enjoyed the programme
Measuring results only for participants, in the months after the programme ends
Comparing participants with a similar control group that did not attend
Counting how many people completed the programme
quiz.explanation: A comparable control group shows what would have happened without the programme, which isolates its effect. Satisfaction, completion and after-only measures cannot separate the programme from prices, markets or seasons.

quiz.question: When calculating a programme's fully loaded cost, which item is most often left out but should be included?
options: The trainer's fee for delivering the sessions
Venue hire, refreshments and the AV equipment for every session
Printed materials and workbooks
Participants' salaries for the time they spend away from work
quiz.explanation: Participants' time away from the job is a real cost and often the largest one, yet it is frequently omitted. Facilitator fees, venues and materials are usually counted already.

quiz.question: Which action does most to help supervisors apply a new coaching skill back at work?
options: Making the course a day longer so that more content, practice and case studies can be covered in the classroom
Their manager discusses goals with them before the course and agrees what they will apply afterwards
Giving out certificates at the end of the course
Holding the course at a hotel rather than at the office
quiz.explanation: Manager involvement before and after training is one of the strongest drivers of transfer. Longer courses can increase forgetting, and certificates and venues do little for application.

quiz.question: A new HR director announces: 'Research shows only 10% of learning comes from courses, so we will cut formal training by 90% and rely on experience.' What is the best response?
options: He is right: 70-20-10 is a well-proven rule for splitting learning budgets, and most large companies apply it exactly this way
He should cut formal training completely, since experience provides 70%
70-20-10 applies only to frontline staff, so managers still need full courses
70-20-10 is an approximate guideline, not a budget formula; formal learning works best linked to experience and coaching
quiz.explanation: 70-20-10 came from what successful managers recalled about their learning, and its numbers are approximate. It argues for connecting formal learning to experience and support, not for cutting it. It is not limited to frontline staff.

sessions.title: Career Paths, Potential and Succession Planning
sessions.summary: Tariq retires in eight months and nobody can run the Sundar plant without him. Build career paths, place talent on the 9-box grid, tell performance from potential, plan succession for critical roles and cut key-person risk before the chair is empty.
objectives: Design career paths, including dual career ladders for specialists
Use the 9-box grid to separate performance from potential and choose actions for each group
Identify high potentials using aspiration, ability and engagement, and avoid common errors
Plan succession for critical roles, measure bench strength and reduce key-person risk

cards.title: Eight months
cards.setting: Sundar Industrial Estate, plant office. The hum of the packing lines through the wall.

lines.text: I'll say it plainly. I turn sixty in July and I'm retiring. My wife has already booked Umrah.
Congratulations, Tariq sahib. And who runs Sundar after you?

Waqas is my best engineer, but he hates managing people. Hina in quality is sharp and hungry, but only six years in. And the food authority inspectors, the halal certifier and the boiler contractor all deal only with me.
I checked. Of our 12 critical roles, three have no successor at all. Sundar plant head is one of them.
Not my problem. Just don't touch Rubina. Multan collapses without her.
Everything is everyone's problem when a chair goes empty. Time for a proper talent review.
Your mission: find who can grow, protect the critical roles, and get Tariq's knowledge out of his head before July.

cards.title: Career paths that keep people growing

scenes.heading: Job architecture
scenes.narration: Careers start with structure: job families such as sales or engineering, and levels within each family with clear expectations at every step.

scenes.heading: Vertical moves
scenes.narration: The classic path is up: TSO, area manager, regional manager. But there are only so many boxes at the top.

scenes.heading: Lateral moves
scenes.narration: Lateral moves build breadth: a TSO moving into trade marketing, or an engineer into quality. They grow capability without a promotion.

scenes.heading: The dual ladder
scenes.narration: A dual career ladder lets specialists advance in pay, status and influence without managing people, so you don't lose a great engineer to make a poor manager.

scenes.heading: Mobility
scenes.narration: Internal moves fill roles faster, keep knowledge in the company and tell ambitious people they don't need to leave to grow.

cards.title: Waqas's two ladders
cards.caption: Both tracks reach senior grades with comparable pay; they differ in what people lead.

items.label: Risk if forced
items.left: Great engineer becomes an unhappy manager

cards.question: Waqas is the plant's best engineer and wants to keep growing, but does not want to manage people. What should Noor Valley offer?
options: The plant head job, since he is the best performer
Progression on a specialist track with senior technical roles
Nothing, since growth always means managing people
A lateral move into sales to broaden him
cards.explanation: A dual career ladder lets specialists grow in grade, pay and influence without managing people. Promoting the best technician into management against his wishes often loses a great engineer and gains an unhappy manager.

cards.title: The 9-box grid
cards.body:
The 9-box grid plots people on two axes, each rated low, moderate or high:
- **Performance** (horizontal): results and behaviours in the *current* role, from appraisal evidence.
- **Potential** (vertical): capacity to grow into *bigger, more complex* roles in future.

Key boxes and typical actions:
- **High performance, high potential**: future leaders. Stretch roles, exposure, succession slates, retention focus.
- **High potential, low performance**: the 'rough diamond' or misfit. Find out why: new in role, wrong role, poor manager? Coach or move, then review.
- **High performance, low potential**: trusted professionals. Recognise, retain and deepen expertise; don't push them up against their wishes.
- **Low performance, low potential**: address through a PIP or a better-fitting role.
- **The middle**: core players who keep the business running; develop and engage them.

Box labels vary between companies. The grid is a snapshot for discussion, not a permanent label.

cards.title: Performance or potential? Myths and facts

cards.front: Myth: every top performer is a high potential.
cards.back: Most high potentials perform well, but many strong performers do not want, or are not suited to, bigger roles. Performance is about now; potential is about the future.
A widely used view combines aspiration (wants a bigger role), ability (can handle more complexity) and engagement (committed to staying).
The ability and willingness to learn from experience and apply it in new, unfamiliar situations. A strong signal of potential.
Aspiration and engagement change with life events and treatment at work. Review potential at least yearly.
A panel in a talent review, using evidence from several sources, not a single manager alone.

cards.front: Myth: the 9-box rating is the person.
cards.back: It is one review's snapshot. Used as a permanent label, it limits people and invites bias.

cards.title: Evidence of what?
cards.prompt: Sort Zoya's notes from the talent review.

items.text: Hit 128% of her sales target this year
Learned the trade-marketing tools in weeks when covering a vacancy
Says she wants to lead a region within three years
Lowest distributor overdue days in the region
Seeks feedback and changes approach after setbacks
Opened 140 new outlets against a goal of 100
Handled an unfamiliar crisis well when the Sukkur depot flooded
Rated 'exceeds' on all KPIs in calibration

cards.title: The talent review
cards.setting: Boardroom. A 9-box grid on the screen, names on sticky notes.

lines.text: Rubina: high performance, and every potential signal is strong: aspiration, learning agility, she ran the depot flood response herself.
Don't put her in any talent pool. If she moves, Multan collapses. I'll keep her happy with a bonus.
(message to you on WhatsApp, earlier that morning) A rival has asked me to meet. I don't want to leave, but I've been in Multan for six years with no path.
Bilal, if we hold her back, we don't keep her. We lose her to someone who will grow her.
(on the line) And Hina in quality has the same pattern. High potential, newer, needs stretch.
Then let's do this properly: critical roles, successors, readiness, and a plan for each.

cards.title: Bilal's talent hoarding
cards.situation: Bilal blocks Rubina's nomination to the regional manager talent pool because Multan's numbers depend on her. Rubina has told you, in confidence, that a rival has approached her and that she feels stuck. As Talent Lead, what do you do?

choices.text: Respect Bilal's decision; he is her manager and Multan's results matter.
choices.outcome: Rubina accepts the rival's offer two months later. Bilal loses her anyway, and the company loses a future regional leader. Hoarding talent rarely keeps it.

choices.text: Tell Bilal about the rival approach so he understands the urgency.
choices.outcome: Rubina shared it in confidence. Breaking that trust may push her out faster, and it treats the symptom without fixing her lack of a path.

choices.text: Raise it in the talent review: talent belongs to the company, so nominate Rubina, agree a development plan and build a successor for Multan.
choices.outcome: The review agrees that Rubina joins the pool with a stretch assignment and a mentor, and her strongest TSO is developed as Multan's successor. Bilal's results are protected by a plan, not by blocking her. Right approach.

choices.text: Offer Rubina a one-off bonus to stay in Multan.
choices.outcome: Money may buy time, but her reason for looking is lack of growth. Without a path, the next offer will tempt her again.

cards.title: Succession planning step by step
cards.caption: Focus on a small number of critical roles rather than every job.

items.label: Identify critical roles
items.detail: High business impact and hard to fill quickly.

items.label: Define success profiles
items.detail: Experience, skills and behaviours the role will need.

items.label: Assess candidates
items.detail: Evidence from performance, potential and talent reviews.

items.label: Rate readiness
items.detail: Ready now, ready in 1-2 years, or 3-5 years; name an emergency cover.

items.label: Develop successors
items.detail: Stretch roles, mentoring and targeted learning.

items.label: Review regularly
items.detail: Update at least yearly and after any major change.

cards.title: Key-person risk map
cards.caption: Plot each critical role-holder by the likelihood of losing them and the impact if you did.

items.label: Protect and document
items.detail: High impact, low likelihood: name a successor, capture knowledge.

items.label: Act now
items.detail: High impact, high likelihood: successor, knowledge transfer and retention plan.

items.label: Monitor
items.detail: Low impact, low likelihood: normal review cycle.

items.label: Plan backfill
items.detail: Low impact, high likelihood: keep a hiring or cover plan ready.

cards.question: Zoya scores key-person risk as likelihood of loss (1-5) × impact of loss (1-5). Tariq's retirement is confirmed and his role is critical. Which score and action fit?
options: 5 + 5 = 10: monitor
5 × 1 = 5: plan backfill
5 × 5 = 25: act now
1 × 5 = 5: protect and document
cards.explanation: A confirmed retirement makes likelihood 5, and the plant head's impact is 5, so the score is 25, in the high-impact, high-likelihood 'act now' quadrant.

cards.title: Noor Valley's bench strength
cards.caption: Ready-now coverage = critical roles with at least one ready-now successor ÷ all critical roles.

items.label: Critical roles
items.detail: High impact and hard to fill quickly.

items.label: Ready-now coverage
items.detail: Roles with at least one ready-now successor.

items.label: Ready in 1-2 years only
items.detail: Successors named but not yet ready.

items.label: No successor
items.detail: Including Sundar plant head: the top priority.

cards.title: Readiness at Sundar
cards.body:
The review rates candidates for plant head:

- **Hina Shah, Quality Manager**: high potential, strong on food safety and people; little experience of maintenance and budgets. **Ready in 1-2 years**.
- **Waqas Ali, Senior Engineer**: superb technically; low aspiration to manage. **Not a successor**; moved onto the specialist track as principal engineer instead.
- **External option**: an experienced plant head could be hired. Faster, but costly and with culture risk.

Tariq retires in eight months, so nobody is **ready now**. The plan:
- Name the production manager as **emergency (interim) successor** who can hold the role safely if Tariq left suddenly.
- Accelerate Hina with a stretch assignment running maintenance and budgets, and Tariq as her mentor.
- Agree a short **post-retirement advisory contract** with Tariq.
- Start a parallel external search as a fallback.

Succession is about options and risk, not one name in a box.

cards.title: Get Tariq's knowledge out of his head
cards.prompt: Put Farzana's knowledge-transfer plan for Tariq in order.
steps: Map the critical knowledge, decisions and relationships only Tariq holds
Name the successor and an emergency cover for the role
Document explicit knowledge: procedures, supplier terms, audit and certification files
Pair Hina with Tariq: she shadows him, then leads while he observes and coaches
Introduce Hina personally to inspectors, the halal certifier and key contractors
Release Tariq's retention bonus as each transfer milestone is completed
Hand over, with an agreed advisory period after retirement

cards.question: Twelve critical roles: 7 have a ready-now successor, 2 have successors ready in 1-2 years, and 3 have none. Zoya says 'our succession coverage is 75%.' What is wrong?
options: Nothing; 9 of 12 roles have a named successor
Coverage should be 25%, the share with no successor
Coverage should count every employee in the company
Ready-now coverage is 58%; 75% counts successors who are not yet ready
cards.explanation: Nine of 12 roles (75%) have someone named, but only 7 of 12 (58%) have a successor who could step in now. Bench strength reports should separate ready-now coverage from longer-term readiness.

cards.title: Talent pools, transparency and fairness
cards.body:
- **Talent pools** develop a group of people for a family of roles (for example, 'future regional managers'), which is more flexible than naming one replacement per job. Use them when roles change fast.
- **Tell people where they stand**, carefully. Hidden lists breed rumours; overpromising breeds entitlement. Talk about development and opportunity, not guaranteed promotions.
- **Fight hoarding**: talent belongs to the organisation. Recognise managers who grow and export people.
- **Check fairness**: look at who gets nominated by gender, location and background. Panels and evidence reduce bias.

cards.title: Stage four cleared: the chair has a plan
items: Career architecture needs vertical, lateral and specialist (dual ladder) paths so people can grow without leaving or becoming reluctant managers.
The 9-box separates current performance from future potential; it is a snapshot for discussion, not a label.
Potential combines aspiration, ability and engagement; learning agility is a strong signal; not every top performer is a high potential.
Succession focuses on critical roles: rate readiness, name emergency cover, report ready-now coverage honestly.
Key-person risk = likelihood × impact. Transfer tacit knowledge through shadowing and introductions, and tie retention bonuses to milestones.

cards.prompt: Name one role in your organisation that would cause real damage if its holder left next month. Who could cover it now, who could hold it in two years, and what knowledge would walk out of the door with them?

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of a dual career ladder?
options: To give every employee two reporting managers, one for daily work and one for career, for better oversight
To allow two people to share one senior role
To let specialists progress in grade, pay and influence without having to manage people
To move people between two companies in the same group
quiz.explanation: A dual ladder provides a specialist track parallel to the management track, so technical experts can advance without becoming reluctant managers.

quiz.question: On a 9-box grid, what do the two axes measure?
options: Performance in the current role and potential for bigger future roles
Salary and length of service
Engagement score and absence rate
Technical skills against the job profile, and formal qualifications held
quiz.explanation: The 9-box plots current performance against future potential. Pay, tenure, engagement and qualifications may inform the discussion, but they are not the axes.
