quiz.question: A senior engineer consistently delivers excellent results, is respected for his expertise, and has said clearly that he does not want a bigger management role. Where does he likely sit on the 9-box, and what is the best action?
options: High performance, high potential: promote him to plant head at the next opening
High performance, lower potential: recognise, retain and deepen his expertise
Low performance, high potential: coach him for a new role
Low performance, low potential: start a PIP
quiz.explanation: Strong current results with low aspiration for bigger roles places him as a high performer with lower potential (a trusted professional). The right action is to recognise and retain him, not push him into management.

quiz.question: Which three elements make up a widely used view of potential?
options: Tenure, salary and qualifications
Performance, attendance and punctuality
Aspiration, ability and engagement
Popularity, confidence and visibility
quiz.explanation: A common model defines potential as aspiration (wanting bigger roles), ability (handling more complexity) and engagement (commitment to the organisation). Confidence and visibility are often mistaken for potential.

quiz.question: Which role is most clearly a 'critical role' for succession planning?
options: Receptionist at head office: important for first impressions
Data-entry clerk: one of many people in the team who do the same job
Driver for the Lahore office: easy to hire within days
Sundar plant head: major business impact and hard to fill quickly
quiz.explanation: Critical roles combine high business impact with scarcity or long lead times to fill. The other roles matter, but they can be filled or covered quickly.

quiz.question: What does it mean to rate a successor 'ready now'?
options: They could step into the role immediately and perform it with normal support
They might be ready after another two years of development
They have the right qualifications on paper but no relevant hands-on experience
They are the most senior person in the team
quiz.explanation: 'Ready now' means able to take the role immediately. 'Ready in 1-2 years' or '3-5 years' describe candidates who need more development. Seniority alone is not readiness.

quiz.question: A bank has 15 critical roles. Six have at least one ready-now successor, 5 have successors ready in 1-2 years, and 4 have none. What is its ready-now coverage?
quiz.explanation: Ready-now coverage = 6 ÷ 15 = 40%. The 73% figure (11 ÷ 15) counts successors who are not yet ready, and 27% is the share with no successor.

quiz.question: A key distributor manager has resigned verbally and is negotiating with a rival. His role holds major customer relationships. Where does he sit on the key-person risk map?
options: High impact, high likelihood: act now
High impact, low likelihood: protect and document
Low impact, high likelihood: plan backfill
Low impact, low likelihood: monitor
quiz.explanation: A likely departure from a high-impact role is in the 'act now' quadrant: secure cover, transfer relationships and decide quickly on any retention response.

quiz.question: A regional manager refuses to nominate his strongest area manager for the leadership pool because 'my region will suffer if she moves'. What is this, and what is the best response?
options: Good retention practice; support the manager's decision, since keeping her in place protects the region's results
Similar-to-me bias; ask another manager to rate her
Talent hoarding; treat talent as the organisation's, nominate her and build a successor for her role
Central tendency; recalibrate her performance rating
quiz.explanation: Blocking a strong person's growth to protect local results is talent hoarding. It usually ends with the person leaving. The fix is to develop her and build a successor so the region is protected by a plan.

quiz.question: Noor Valley's regional manager roles are being redesigned as the company moves to digital distribution, so the exact future roles are unclear. Which succession approach suits this best?
options: Name one specific replacement for each current regional manager
Build a talent pool of future regional leaders developed for broad capabilities
Pause all succession planning until the new roles are fully defined
Hire external regional managers now so they are in place to fill the future roles
quiz.explanation: When roles are changing, a talent pool develops a group of people with broad capabilities, giving flexibility. One-to-one replacement planning assumes today's role will stay the same, and pausing leaves the company exposed.

sessions.title: Engagement, Retention, Rewards, Inclusion and Talent Analytics
sessions.summary: A rival is courting Rubina, women TSOs are leaving at twice the rate of men, and the board wants the talent story in numbers. Cost turnover, run stay interviews, use total rewards and pay data, build inclusion, and turn HR data into analytics leaders act on.
objectives: Explain why people stay and leave, run stay interviews and read flight-risk signals
Calculate the cost of turnover and core retention metrics
Apply total rewards, compa-ratio and range penetration to retention decisions
Build inclusion with evidence, including adverse-impact checks, within Pakistan's legal framework
Use talent analytics responsibly, from descriptive to prescriptive, and present it to leadership

cards.title: The offer letter
cards.setting: Your phone, 10:42 pm. A WhatsApp message from Multan.

lines.text: Sorry to message so late. The rival sent a written offer today: regional role, 30% more pay, a car. They want an answer by Friday.
I don't want to leave. But I have been in Multan six years. Nobody has asked me what I want.
Next morning, Bilal storms into the people team's room.
Match it! Whatever they offer, add ten percent. I can't lose her.
And she isn't the only one. Women TSOs are leaving at twice the rate of men, and the board wants our talent numbers in three weeks.
Final stage. Keep the people who matter, understand why others go, and tell the board the truth in numbers.
Start with Rubina. And not with money.

cards.title: Why people stay, and why they go

scenes.heading: Push and pull
scenes.narration: People leave because something pushes them, like a poor manager or no growth, and something pulls them, like a better offer. Pull factors rarely work without a push.

scenes.heading: The manager effect
scenes.narration: The direct manager shapes most of what people feel about work: fairness, recognition, growth and workload. Many resignations are really about the manager.

scenes.heading: Hygiene factors
scenes.narration: Herzberg's hygiene factors, such as pay, conditions, policies and supervision, cause dissatisfaction when poor. Fixing them removes complaints but does not create motivation.

scenes.heading: Motivators
scenes.narration: Motivators, such as achievement, recognition, responsibility, growth and interesting work, are what actually build satisfaction and commitment.

scenes.heading: Focus on regrettable loss
scenes.narration: Not all turnover is bad. Voluntary leavers you wanted to keep are regrettable turnover. That is where retention effort pays.

cards.title: What it costs to lose an area manager
cards.caption: Rubina's role: annual salary PKR 4.8m. Estimates vary by role; commonly quoted ranges run from about half to twice annual salary.

items.label: Separation
items.detail: Exit administration, final settlement processing and handover time.

items.label: Vacancy
items.detail: Margin lost while the territory has no manager, net of salary saved.

items.label: Recruitment
items.detail: Agency fee at 15% of annual salary, plus interview time.

items.label: Onboarding and training
items.detail: Induction, travel and training for the new manager.

items.label: Ramp-up
items.detail: Lower output while the new manager learns the territory.

items.label: Total cost of one exit
items.detail: About 79% of annual salary.

cards.question: Losing one TSO costs: recruitment PKR 0.18m, vacancy PKR 0.40m, training PKR 0.12m and ramp-up PKR 0.90m. The TSO's annual salary is PKR 1.2m. What is the total cost, as a share of salary?
options: PKR 1.6m, about 133% of annual salary
PKR 0.7m, about 58% of annual salary
PKR 1.2m, exactly 100% of annual salary
PKR 1.6m, about 75% of annual salary
cards.explanation: Total = 0.18 + 0.40 + 0.12 + 0.90 = PKR 1.6m. As a share of salary, 1.6 ÷ 1.2 ≈ 133%. Leaving out ramp-up (PKR 0.7m) is the most common way turnover cost is understated.

cards.title: Stay interviews and flight risk
cards.body:
An **exit interview** asks why someone is leaving, when it is too late. A **stay interview** asks valued people, while they are still here, what keeps them and what might pull them away.

Good stay-interview questions:
- What do you look forward to most at work? What frustrates you?
- What would make you think about leaving?
- What would you like to learn or do next?
- What could I, as your manager, do differently?

The manager runs it, listens more than talks, and **acts on one or two things quickly**. Promising everything and doing nothing is worse than not asking.

**Flight-risk signals** to watch:
- Triggers: passed over for promotion, a new manager, a restructure, long time in role, pay below market.
- Behaviour changes: less discretionary effort, withdrawing from meetings, sudden interest in documenting their own work.

Base judgements on evidence, never on assumptions about gender, marital status or age.

cards.title: Flight-risk signal or not?
cards.prompt: Zoya reviews notes from managers. Sort each item.
buckets: Not a reliable signal on its own

items.text: Passed over for the regional role she was promised last year
Six years in the same role with no development move
Paid well below the midpoint of her grade's range
Took her planned annual leave in December
Stopped volunteering for projects and skips optional team calls
Recently got married
Her trusted manager has just left and a new manager has arrived
Asked a question about the gratuity policy during an HR briefing

cards.title: Rubina's Friday deadline
cards.situation: Rubina has a written offer: a regional role, 30% more pay and a car, with an answer due Friday. Bilal wants to match the pay plus 10%. In your stay conversation, Rubina says her main reasons are six years without growth and feeling unheard. The talent review has already placed her in the regional leadership pool. What do you recommend?

choices.text: Match the offer plus 10%, as Bilal suggests, and close the conversation.
choices.outcome: She may stay for now, but the real push (no growth, not heard) is untouched. Counteroffers made under pressure also create pay inequity, and the next offer will tempt her again.

choices.text: Let her go; anyone who considers leaving is no longer loyal.
choices.outcome: You lose a future regional leader and at least PKR 3.8m in turnover cost. Being approached by rivals is a sign of talent, not disloyalty.

choices.text: Offer a concrete development path: a stretch regional assignment now, the leadership pool, a mentor, and a pay review against the range. Fix what pushed her, and put it in writing.
choices.outcome: Rubina sees a real future and a fair pay review. She declines the rival. You fixed the push factors, not just the pull. Right approach: stay interviews and growth beat reactive counteroffers.

choices.text: Tell her that leaving within a year of a bonus means repaying it.
choices.outcome: Threats may delay her exit but destroy trust. She leaves at the first chance and tells others why.

cards.title: Total rewards and pay position
cards.body:
**Total rewards** is everything people value from working with you:
- **Pay**: base salary, allowances, incentives and bonuses.
- **Benefits**: medical cover, provident fund, gratuity, EOBI and social security contributions, car or fuel policy, loans.
- **Wellbeing and work environment**: flexibility, safety, transport, workload.
- **Development and career**: learning, mobility, promotion.
- **Recognition**: being noticed and thanked, formally and informally.

Two pay measures help explain retention risk:
- **Compa-ratio** = salary ÷ midpoint of the pay range. 1.00 means paid at the midpoint; below about 0.90 often flags underpayment for an experienced performer.
- **Range penetration** = (salary − range minimum) ÷ (range maximum − range minimum). It shows how far up the range someone is.

Pay fixes hygiene problems; growth and recognition build commitment. Use both, and check current tax and benefits rules before designing packages.

cards.title: Rubina's pay position
cards.caption: Area manager pay range (monthly): minimum PKR 320k, midpoint PKR 400k, maximum PKR 480k.

items.label: Rubina's salary
items.detail: Monthly base pay after six years.

items.label: Compa-ratio
items.detail: 380k ÷ 400k midpoint.

items.label: Rival's offer
items.detail: 30% more: above the top of her current range.

cards.question: A TSO earns PKR 90,000 a month. The TSO pay range has a midpoint of PKR 100,000. What is his compa-ratio, and what does it suggest?
options: 1.10: paid 10% above the midpoint
0.90: paid 10% below the midpoint
0.10: almost unpaid relative to the range
0.90: paid at the top of the range
cards.explanation: Compa-ratio = 90,000 ÷ 100,000 = 0.90, meaning he is paid 10% below the midpoint. It does not say where the range ends; range penetration would show that.

cards.title: Twice the rate
cards.setting: People analytics corner. Zoya has three charts open.

lines.text: Women TSOs: 32% attrition. Men: 16%. And among applicants, we hire 20% of women and 40% of men.
Women just don't like field sales. That's the reality.
The exit data says otherwise. The top reasons are late-evening market visits without transport and two complaints about one supervisor that went nowhere.
(on the call) In Multan I scheduled market visits before sunset and arranged shared transport. My two women TSOs are my top performers.
Two complaints that went nowhere is a legal and moral failure. That goes to the inquiry committee today.
Then we fix the system, not the women.

cards.title: Inclusion vocabulary
cards.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: The mix of people in a team: gender, age, region, background, disability and more
Whether those people are respected, heard and able to contribute and progress
Fair access and treatment, which may mean removing barriers some groups face
A practice that selects one group at a substantially lower rate than another
Comparing pay for similar work across groups, adjusting for legitimate factors

cards.title: Pakistan's legal anchors for inclusion
cards.body:
Pointers only: check current law and take advice.
- **Harassment**: the Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act 2010 (as amended) requires a displayed code of conduct and an inquiry committee with at least one woman. Handle complaints; never bury them.
- **Disability**: federal and provincial laws set employment quotas; check your province's current figure.
- **Gender identity**: the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 addresses discrimination in employment; parts have faced court challenge, so check its current status.
- **Maternity and paternity leave** rules differ federally and by province.

cards.title: From reporting to recommending
cards.caption: Most HR teams live at the first level. Value grows as you move right, with more data and more care.

items.label: Descriptive
items.detail: What happened? Headcount, attrition, time-to-fill.

items.label: Diagnostic
items.detail: Why did it happen? Exit reasons, cuts by manager or region.

items.label: Predictive
items.detail: What is likely to happen? Flight-risk models, hiring needs.

items.label: Prescriptive
items.detail: What should we do? Recommended actions and their expected effect.

cards.back: Voluntary: the employee chooses to leave. Involuntary: the employer ends employment, for example dismissal or redundancy.
Regrettable leavers (people you wanted to keep) ÷ all leavers. Shows how much of your turnover really hurts.
A quarter's attrition rate × 4 gives a rough annual equivalent; a month's × 12. Seasonal patterns can distort it.
Employees answer 0-10: would you recommend us as a place to work? % promoters (9-10) minus % detractors (0-6). Passives (7-8) are left out.
If a group's selection rate is below 80% of the highest group's rate, investigate possible adverse impact. Originally a US guideline.
Probability of leaving × full turnover cost. Compare how much a retention action lowers this expected cost with what the action itself costs.
Two things moving together does not prove one causes the other. Volunteers, for example, may differ from non-volunteers before any programme starts.
Never report survey or analytics results for groups so small that individuals can be identified; many firms use a minimum of 5 to 10.

cards.title: Noor Valley's first eNPS
cards.caption: Question: 'How likely are you to recommend Noor Valley as a place to work?' 300 responses.

items.label: Promoters
items.detail: Scored 9 or 10.

items.label: Passives
items.detail: Scored 7 or 8: not counted.

items.label: Detractors
items.detail: Scored 0 to 6.

items.label: eNPS
items.detail: 40% promoters minus 30% detractors.

cards.question: In a Karachi office survey, 50 of 200 respondents score 9-10, 70 score 7-8 and 80 score 0-6. What is the eNPS?
cards.explanation: Promoters are 25% (50 ÷ 200) and detractors 40% (80 ÷ 200). eNPS = 25 − 40 = −15. Passives are excluded, and the score is a difference of percentages, not a count.

cards.title: Run a talent analytics project
cards.prompt: Put Zoya's steps for the women-TSO attrition study in order.
steps: Agree the business question with leaders: why are women TSOs leaving faster?
Gather data: HR records, exit interviews, survey results and complaint logs
Clean the data and protect privacy, removing names and small groups
Analyse patterns by region, manager, tenure and shift timing
Turn findings into a short story with recommended actions
Agree actions with leaders and measure the change over the next two quarters

cards.title: Zoya's adverse-impact check
cards.body:
Zoya compares TSO hiring outcomes for the last year:

| Group | Applicants | Hired | Selection rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Men | 120 | 48 | 40% |
| Women | 60 | 12 | 20% |

**Impact ratio** = 20% ÷ 40% = **0.50**, far below the four-fifths (0.80) rule of thumb. That is not proof of discrimination, but it demands investigation.

She finds two causes. A phone screen asked 'Can you work until 10 pm?' and screened out most women, though late visits were rare and could be scheduled. And all-male panels rated 'confidence' heavily.

The fixes: job-related screening questions only, mixed panels, structured scoring, and visits planned before sunset with shared transport. Six months later, the ratio is 0.86.

Correlation is a clue, not a verdict: always test the cause before acting.

cards.title: The night before the board
cards.setting: Farzana's office, 8:30 pm. The board pack is printed.

lines.text: (voice note) I said no to the rival. Starting the Sukkur regional assignment on the first of next month.
Hina ran the plant alone this week while I watched. She caught a boiler fault I would have missed. Maybe I can retire after all.
My region's 90-day attrition is down to 8%. I hate to admit it, but the structured interviews and buddies work.
And women TSO attrition is falling. The dashboard is ready: hiring, early attrition, calibration, ROI, bench strength, eNPS.
Tomorrow the board will test everything we have built. Every number must be honest, and every number must lead to a decision.
You have filled the empty chairs. Now face the final boss.

cards.title: Stage five cleared: ready for the board
items: People leave when a push meets a pull; managers, growth and recognition matter more than pay alone once hygiene factors are fair.
Cost turnover fully: separation, vacancy, recruitment, onboarding and ramp-up. Focus effort on regrettable losses.
Stay interviews and fixing push factors beat reactive counteroffers.
Compa-ratio = salary ÷ midpoint; range penetration = (salary − min) ÷ (max − min); eNPS = % promoters − % detractors.
Check selection rates with the four-fifths rule of thumb, follow Pakistan's harassment and equality laws, and fix systems, not people.
Analytics moves from descriptive to prescriptive; protect privacy, avoid tiny groups, and never confuse correlation with causation.

cards.prompt: Which two people on your team would hurt most to lose? When did you last ask them what keeps them here and what might pull them away? Draft the first three questions of a stay interview you could hold this month.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of a stay interview?
options: To learn what keeps valued employees and what might pull them away, while there is still time to act
To find out, after an employee has resigned, which reasons led to the decision and what the company could learn
To decide whether an employee's contract should be renewed
To assess a new hire's performance at the end of probation
quiz.explanation: A stay interview is held with valued people before they think of leaving, so problems can be fixed. Asking why someone already resigned is an exit interview.

quiz.question: Losing one sales supervisor costs: separation PKR 0.05m, vacancy PKR 0.6m, recruitment PKR 0.3m, onboarding PKR 0.15m and ramp-up PKR 0.9m. Her annual salary is PKR 2.5m. What is the total cost of her exit as a share of salary?
quiz.explanation: Total = 0.05 + 0.6 + 0.3 + 0.15 + 0.9 = PKR 2.0m. As a share of salary, 2.0 ÷ 2.5 = 80%. Forgetting ramp-up gives PKR 1.1m, or 44%.

quiz.question: Last year 30 people left a division voluntarily. Managers say 12 of them were people they had wanted to keep. What is the regrettable turnover share?
quiz.explanation: Regrettable share = regrettable leavers ÷ all leavers = 12 ÷ 30 = 40%. The other 18 (60%) were leavers the company did not regret losing.

quiz.question: Noor Valley raises salaries to market level and improves office facilities. Complaints drop, but engagement scores barely move. What does Herzberg's model suggest?
options: The pay rise was simply too small: engagement always rises in line with pay once increases are large enough to be noticed
Engagement surveys cannot detect changes in pay
Facilities are motivators, so they should have raised engagement
Pay and conditions are hygiene factors: fixing them cuts dissatisfaction, but growth and recognition drive engagement
quiz.explanation: Herzberg separates hygiene factors (pay, conditions, policies), which prevent dissatisfaction, from motivators (achievement, recognition, growth, responsibility), which drive satisfaction. The result fits that model.

quiz.question: An area manager earns PKR 225,000 a month. The range for her grade runs from PKR 200,000 to PKR 300,000, with a midpoint of PKR 250,000. What is her compa-ratio?
quiz.explanation: Compa-ratio = salary ÷ midpoint = 225,000 ÷ 250,000 = 0.90. Her range penetration would be (225 − 200) ÷ (300 − 200) = 25%, a different measure.

quiz.question: An engagement survey of 200 staff finds 70 promoters (9-10), 80 passives (7-8) and 50 detractors (0-6). What is the eNPS?
quiz.explanation: Promoters = 35%, detractors = 25%. eNPS = 35 − 25 = +10. Passives are excluded. The figure 35 is just the promoter share.

quiz.question: A bank hires 30 of 100 male applicants and 9 of 60 female applicants for teller roles. Using the four-fifths rule of thumb, what should HR conclude?
options: The impact ratio is 0.30, which proves that the bank is discriminating unlawfully and must change its process at once
There is no concern, because the bank hired 9 women
The impact ratio is 0.50, below 0.80, so the selection process should be investigated for adverse impact
The impact ratio is 0.80, exactly at the threshold, so no action is needed
quiz.explanation: Selection rates are 30% for men and 15% for women. Impact ratio = 15 ÷ 30 = 0.50, below the 0.80 rule of thumb, so the process needs investigation. A low ratio is a warning sign, not proof of unlawful discrimination.

quiz.question: A team has a good mix of genders, regions and ages, but in meetings the same two senior men make every decision and others' ideas are ignored. What is missing?
options: Diversity
Inclusion
Compliance
Representation
quiz.explanation: The team is diverse (a varied mix of people), but not inclusive: people are not heard or able to contribute. Representation describes the mix, which is already present.

quiz.question: Zoya builds a model that uses tenure, pay position and recent manager changes to estimate which TSOs are likely to leave in the next six months. Which level of analytics is this?
options: Descriptive
Diagnostic
Prescriptive
Predictive
quiz.explanation: Estimating what is likely to happen is predictive analytics. Descriptive reports what happened, diagnostic explains why, and prescriptive recommends what to do.

quiz.question: A woman TSO tells her manager that a supervisor sends her inappropriate WhatsApp messages. Under Pakistan's workplace harassment law, what should the company do?
options: Refer the complaint to the organisation's harassment inquiry committee and protect her from retaliation
Ask her to resolve it directly with the supervisor first
Transfer her quietly to another territory so that she no longer works with him, and then close the matter
Wait for a second complaint before taking any action
quiz.explanation: The harassment law requires employers to have a code of conduct and an inquiry committee to deal with complaints. Moving the complainant, asking her to confront the supervisor or waiting for more complaints fails her and the law. Check current law for procedural details.

bank.question: Noor Valley plans to launch a new frozen-foods division next year. The company has never sold frozen products, timing depends on a cold-chain partner, and nobody can say whether launch will be in March or September. Which demand-forecasting approach suits this best?
options: Ratio analysis using the current number of TSOs per active outlet in the dry-goods business, applied to the frozen range
Scenario planning with expected, early and delayed launch cases, refined with experienced managers' judgement
Trend analysis of the last five years of headcount growth across the company
Waiting until the launch date is confirmed before doing any workforce planning
bank.explanation: With no history and high uncertainty, scenario planning (combined with managerial judgement) is the right tool. Ratio and trend methods assume the future looks like the past, which does not hold for a new category. Waiting removes the lead time needed to hire.

bank.question: A Karachi customer contact centre has 120 agents. It needs 150 by December, expects attrition of 40% on today's headcount, and knows 6 agents will transfer to the new Hyderabad centre. How many agents must it hire this year?
bank.explanation: Growth is 30 (150 minus 120). Expected leavers are 48 (40% of 120). Transfers out are another 6 that must be replaced. Total hires = 30 + 48 + 6 = 84. Forgetting the transfers gives 78.

bank.question: The contact centre must make 84 hires. Offer acceptance is 70% and 30% of interviewees receive offers. How many interviews must it schedule?
bank.explanation: Offers needed = 84 ÷ 0.7 = 120. Interviews needed = 120 ÷ 0.3 = 400. The figure 120 is the number of offers, not interviews; multiplying instead of dividing gives far too few.

bank.question: In three years Noor Valley will need data analysts for its distributor network. Analysts are scarce and expensive in Lahore, but several sales-operations staff already work with spreadsheets and want to grow. Which option should lead the plan?
options: Buy: recruit senior analysts from the market now and hold them in other roles until needed
Borrow: rely on consultants every year for the analysis
Build: develop the sales-operations staff through a structured analytics programme
Bounce: exit the sales-operations staff and replace them later
bank.explanation: With a three-year lead time, scarce external supply and motivated internal staff with adjacent skills, building is the most economical and sustainable option. Buying now pays premium salaries years early, and borrowing creates permanent dependence.

bank.question: Noor Valley's recruitment ads promise 'a relaxed, flexible role with fast promotion'. TSOs actually visit about 45 shops a day on tight targets, and many resign within two months saying the job was 'not what we were told'. What is the best fix?
options: Rebuild the EVP from research with current TSOs and add a realistic job preview before offers
Raise the joining bonus and add a clawback, so that new hires stay at least long enough to avoid repaying it
Shorten the interview so that candidates do not lose interest
Stop exit interviews because they encourage negative feedback
bank.explanation: Early exits caused by a gap between promise and reality are fixed by making the EVP true and giving candidates an honest preview of the job. A bonus clawback treats the symptom and can trap unhappy people, and the other options ignore the cause.

bank.question: An interviewer meets a very weak candidate at 2 pm and an average one at 3 pm. She rates the 3 pm candidate 4.5 out of 5, although his answers match the 'adequate' anchors. Which error is most likely?
options: Halo effect
Similar-to-me bias
Severity error
Contrast effect
bank.explanation: Judging a candidate against the previous one, instead of against the anchored standard, is the contrast effect. Halo would require one trait spilling into other ratings, and severity would push ratings down, not up.

bank.question: Within two minutes a panel member decides a candidate is 'not a sales type'. For the rest of the interview he asks only about the candidate's failures and notes each hesitation, while skipping questions on successes. Which bias best describes how he is gathering evidence?
options: Central tendency
Confirmation bias
Similar-to-me bias
Leniency error
bank.explanation: The early judgement is a first-impression error, but what he is now doing (seeking and noticing only evidence that supports his view) is confirmation bias. Central tendency and leniency are rating patterns, and nothing suggests he is favouring someone like himself.

bank.question: A three-person panel has just finished a structured interview. What should happen next?
options: The most senior member gives a view first so that the others can align with it
The panel first discusses its overall feeling about the candidate, then fills in each score so that it matches that view
Each member scores independently with evidence, then the panel discusses differences and agrees final ratings
Only the line manager scores, because the others are there to observe
bank.explanation: Independent scoring before discussion prevents the most senior or most vocal person from anchoring everyone else. Filling scores in to match a feeling defeats the purpose of anchored scales.

bank.question: Last year Noor Valley spent PKR 1.8m on agency fees, PKR 0.6m on job ads and assessment tools, and PKR 1.2m on the internal recruiting team's time. It made 45 hires. What was its cost-per-hire?
bank.explanation: Total recruiting cost = 1.8 + 0.6 + 1.2 = PKR 3.6m. Divided by 45 hires = PKR 80,000. Leaving out internal recruiter time (PKR 2.4m ÷ 45) gives PKR 53,333, which understates the true cost.

bank.question: After a year of the new structured interview, Bilal wants to prove it works. Which measure gives the most convincing evidence?
options: The average time-to-fill for TSO vacancies this year
The number of applications received per advertisement
Candidates' satisfaction ratings of the new interview experience, collected through a short survey after each interview
Twelve-month performance and retention of TSOs hired through the new process compared with earlier hires
bank.explanation: Quality of hire, shown by new hires' later performance and retention, tests whether selection actually predicts success. Time-to-fill and application volume measure speed and reach, and candidate satisfaction measures experience, not prediction.

bank.question: Exit calls show that new TSOs in remote territories leave mainly because they 'felt alone': they rarely saw their manager and knew nobody to call with a problem. Which onboarding change targets this most directly?
options: Assign a buddy and schedule weekly manager one-to-ones for the first 90 days
Add a longer policy induction on day one that covers every HR rule in detail
Give new hires a printed history of the company and its values
Move their probation review from day 90 to day 60
bank.explanation: The cause is lack of connection, so a buddy and regular manager contact address it directly. A longer policy session is compliance, the company history is culture, and changing the review date does nothing for isolation.

bank.question: A fully productive TSO generates PKR 300,000 gross margin a month. New TSOs average 50% of full output while ramping up. A new onboarding programme cuts time to full productivity from 6 months to 4. For 40 new hires a year, what is the annual value of the faster ramp-up?
options: PKR 24m
PKR 6m
PKR 12m
PKR 36m
bank.explanation: Ramp-up gap per hire falls from 6 × 300,000 × 50% = PKR 900,000 to 4 × 300,000 × 50% = PKR 600,000, a saving of PKR 300,000 per hire. For 40 hires that is PKR 12m. Forgetting the 50% shortfall doubles the figure to PKR 24m.

bank.question: Rubina drafts an OKR: 'Objective: Win Multan's general trade.' Which key result is best written?
options: Visit as many shops as possible every day this quarter
Hold weekly team meetings to discuss general trade
Work harder on building strong, trusting relationships with retailers across every part of Multan this quarter
Increase outlets stocking our full ketchup range in Multan from 1,200 to 1,800 by 31 March
bank.explanation: A key result should be a measurable outcome with a baseline, target and date. Visiting shops and holding meetings are activities, and 'work harder' cannot be measured.

bank.question: For four quarters in a row, every team in Bilal's region scores 1.0 on all its stretch OKRs. What is the most likely interpretation?
options: The objectives are probably not ambitious enough to be real stretch goals
The region has the best performers in the company and needs no review
OKR scoring is broken, so the region should switch back to annual appraisal only
The teams should be rated 'exceeds' automatically on their KPIs too
bank.explanation: Stretch OKRs are designed so that partial achievement (often around 0.6 to 0.7) is healthy. Hitting 1.0 on everything every quarter suggests goals were set safely. It says nothing automatic about KPIs or the scoring method.

bank.question: Analysis shows that when the same TSOs are rated by two different managers, their scores differ more because of who rated them than because of their own results. What does this show, and what is the best response?
options: A recency effect; ask managers to rate only on December's results
An idiosyncratic rater effect; use multiple sources of evidence and calibrate ratings across managers
Similar-to-me bias; ensure managers rate only people from their own city
Central tendency; make every manager use a fixed bell curve so that all regions end up with the same rating spread
bank.explanation: When ratings reveal more about the rater than the ratee, that is the idiosyncratic rater effect. Calibration and multiple evidence sources reduce it. A forced curve does not address which rater is applying the standard wrongly.

bank.question: Noor Valley's policy forces every team to rate its bottom 10% as 'below expectations'. Tariq's six-person engineering team are all meeting demanding standards. What is the main weakness of applying the forced distribution here?
options: It makes calibration meetings unnecessary for engineering
It guarantees that ratings in engineering will end up more lenient than in sales and the other, larger departments
It would label a capable person as underperforming just because the team is small and strong, eroding trust
It stops managers from setting OKRs for their teams
bank.explanation: Forced distributions assume performance always follows a fixed spread, which rarely holds in small or uniformly strong teams. Labelling someone 'below' to fill a quota is unfair and erodes trust. It does not remove the need for calibration.

bank.question: You are facilitating calibration. One manager's ratings are far above every other manager's, while his team's results are average. What should you do first?
options: Restate the rating standard and ask him for specific evidence for each high rating before any change is agreed
Lower all his ratings by one level straight away so that his rating spread matches the company average for the year
Leave his ratings alone, since calibration should not challenge managers
Ask the other managers to raise their ratings to match his
bank.explanation: Good calibration tests ratings against a shared standard with evidence. Mechanically lowering ratings or levelling everyone up skips the evidence, and ignoring the outlier defeats the purpose.

bank.question: A manager tells a TSO: 'You're unprofessional with customers.' Which rewrite best applies SBI?
options: 'You're usually great, but you're unprofessional sometimes, though you're improving.'
'Several people in the region have said that you are unprofessional with customers, so please think about it seriously.'
'You need to show a lot more professionalism and respect towards our customers and distributors if you want to grow in this company.'
'Yesterday at Al-Madina Store you argued with the owner about the scheme in front of customers, and he cancelled this week's order.'
bank.explanation: The first option names the situation, an observable behaviour and its impact. The second is a feedback sandwich with a label, the third is hearsay, and the fourth is still a vague judgement.

bank.question: Bilal wraps every criticism between two compliments. After six months, his team say his praise 'means nothing' and several did not notice they were being corrected. What should he change?
options: Add more compliments before and after each criticism, so that the corrective message lands more softly with the team
Stop giving corrective feedback and save it for the year-end review
Give praise and correction separately and specifically using SBI, then agree next steps with a future focus
Send all feedback by WhatsApp so there is a written record
bank.explanation: The feedback sandwich teaches people to discount praise and miss the message. Separate, specific SBI feedback with a feedforward focus fixes both problems. Saving criticism for year-end creates surprises, and the channel is not the issue.

bank.question: A TSO's PIP ends with targets still missed. The manager wants to terminate immediately, but the file shows no written standards, no record of support offered and no review meetings. What is the soundest advice?
options: Terminate now, because the targets were missed and the outcome is obvious
Reset the PIP with written standards, documented support and scheduled reviews, and take legal advice before any termination
Treat the case as misconduct instead, so that a show-cause notice can be issued quickly and the termination completed this month
Extend the PIP indefinitely without changing anything, to avoid a dispute
bank.explanation: A PIP is only fair and defensible if standards, support and reviews were clear and documented. None were, so the process needs resetting, with advice on the applicable law before termination. Relabelling capability as misconduct is improper, and an open-ended PIP helps nobody.

bank.question: Sales of Noor Valley's new sauce range are falling in Lahore. TSOs scored 90% on a product test and performed strongly in role-plays. The bonus scheme pays a higher rate on the older ketchup range, and stock of the new range often arrives late. What should the needs analysis recommend?
options: Run an advanced product training course, since knowledge always fades
Fix the bonus weighting and the stock supply problem; a product course is unlikely to change results
Run a motivational workshop for all Lahore TSOs to build energy and enthusiasm for selling the new sauce range
Retest the TSOs with a harder exam to find hidden gaps
bank.explanation: TSOs clearly have the knowledge and skill. The causes are incentives and supply, so training would cost money without changing behaviour. A motivational workshop ignores the incentive that drives behaviour.

bank.question: The organisational analysis shows that food-safety capability is critical before an upcoming audit. What should Tariq do next to decide who needs training?
options: Train every employee at the plant on food safety, whether or not their job involves handling food
Ask supervisors which courses they would enjoy
Assess each supervisor against the required food-safety skills to identify individual gaps
Wait for the audit results to see who fails
bank.explanation: Once the organisation and job requirements are clear, individual analysis (assessment, observation, records) shows who lacks the skills. Blanket training wastes money, preferences are not needs, and waiting for the audit is too late.

bank.question: The CEO asks whether last year's supervisor coaching programme 'made any difference to the business'. Which evidence answers his question most directly?
options: Ride-along audits showing that supervisors now coach their TSOs on most visits
Participants' scores on the end-of-course coaching assessment
Feedback forms rating the programme 4.7 out of 5
Sales growth in coached territories compared with similar uncoached territories
bank.explanation: The CEO is asking about business results, Kirkpatrick Level 4, best shown by comparing coached and similar uncoached territories. Ride-along audits are Level 3 (behaviour), which is important but not the business outcome.

bank.question: A negotiation programme shows Level 1 average 4.8 out of 5 and Level 2 scores up from 45% to 85%. Three months later, few participants use the techniques, and their managers say they 'never had time to discuss the course'. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: A transfer problem: involve managers before and after, and give people real negotiations to apply it in
Poor course design: rewrite the content, since such high Level 2 scores show that the course was far too easy
Low engagement: add more energisers and games to raise Level 1 further
Wrong participants: the programme should be stopped and the budget returned
bank.explanation: High reaction and learning with low behaviour change points to the work environment, not the course. Manager involvement and early application drive transfer. Raising Level 1 or rewriting a course that taught well will not help.

bank.question: After a key-account programme, participants' annual margin rose by PKR 12m. Managers estimate that 50% of the improvement came from the programme and are 80% confident in that estimate. The fully loaded cost was PKR 3.0m. What is the programme's ROI?
bank.explanation: Isolated benefit = 12m × 50% × 80% = PKR 4.8m. Net benefit = 4.8 − 3.0 = PKR 1.8m. ROI = 1.8 ÷ 3.0 = 60%. Using the whole PKR 12m gives 300%; skipping the confidence adjustment (PKR 6m) gives 100%.

bank.question: A leadership programme cost PKR 4.0m fully loaded. Its isolated, converted first-year benefits are PKR 3.6m. What are its ROI and BCR, and what do they mean?
options: ROI −10% and BCR 0.9: in year one the programme returned less than it cost
ROI 90% and BCR 0.9: the programme returned most of its cost, which counts as positive
ROI −10% and BCR 1.1: the programme slightly more than paid for itself
ROI 10% and BCR 0.9: the programme made a small profit
bank.explanation: ROI = (3.6 − 4.0) ÷ 4.0 = −10%. BCR = 3.6 ÷ 4.0 = 0.9. Both show a first-year loss. Reporting the BCR as a 90% ROI is a common error; intangible benefits can be reported alongside, but not added to the figure.

bank.question: A two-day workshop for 60 TSOs has these costs: facilitator PKR 0.8m, venue and materials PKR 0.4m, travel and hotels PKR 0.6m. Each TSO's salary cost is PKR 10,000 a day. What is the fully loaded cost?
options: PKR 1.8m
PKR 3.0m
PKR 2.4m
PKR 2.6m
bank.explanation: Direct costs = 0.8 + 0.4 + 0.6 = PKR 1.8m. Participants' time = 60 × 2 days × PKR 10,000 = PKR 1.2m. Fully loaded cost = PKR 3.0m. Leaving out participants' time gives PKR 1.8m.

bank.question: An evaluation of a team-building programme finds better morale in survey comments but no credible way to link it to sales, retention or costs. How should the morale finding be reported?
options: Converted to PKR using an estimate of how happy people feel
Ignored, because anything that cannot be converted to money has no value
Added to the benefits at an assumed value so that the ROI looks positive
As an intangible benefit, reported separately from the ROI figure
bank.explanation: Benefits that cannot be credibly converted to money should be reported as intangibles alongside the ROI, not forced into it. Inventing a value damages credibility, and ignoring them understates the programme's effects.

bank.question: Noor Valley wants to prepare a newly promoted area manager to manage a team of 12 TSOs. Which plan best applies 70-20-10?
options: Send her on a two-week residential management course in Lahore and review her progress at next year's appraisal
Ask her to read three management books over the year
Give her real team responsibilities, a mentor and regular coaching, plus a short people-management course
Let her learn entirely on the job without support, since experience gives 70%
bank.explanation: The best blend combines experience (real responsibilities), learning from others (mentor, coaching) and connected formal learning (a course). The course-only and reading-only options use just the 10%, and the unsupported option drops the 20 and the 10.

bank.question: Tariq's supervisors must master a new allergen procedure and keep using it. Which design is most likely to make the learning stick?
options: A short session, then on-the-job practice with spaced refresher quizzes and supervisor checks over weeks
One full-day session that covers every detail of the procedure thoroughly, with a written test at the end of the day
An e-learning module that staff complete once a year
A printed manual handed out at the start of each shift
bank.explanation: Spaced practice, retrieval and follow-up on the job counter the forgetting curve and build habits. A single long session, a once-a-year module or a manual offers no reinforcement, so much of the learning is forgotten quickly.

bank.question: In a talent review, an area manager is described as follows: exceeds every target, very reliable, struggles when moved to unfamiliar tasks, and says he is happy staying in his city long term. Where should he most likely sit on the 9-box?
options: High performance, high potential
High performance, low or moderate potential
Moderate performance, but high future potential
Low performance, moderate potential
bank.explanation: His current performance is high, but low learning agility in new situations and low aspiration point to lower potential. Treating every top performer as a high potential is the most common 9-box error.

bank.question: A company selects its 'high-potential' list by taking everyone rated 'exceeds' in the last appraisal. What is the main weakness of this method?
options: It selects too few people, because few employees are rated 'exceeds'
It is unfair to managers, who should not be rated
It relies too heavily on peer feedback, which is often unreliable, political and hard to verify
It confuses current performance with potential and ignores aspiration, ability and engagement
bank.explanation: Current performance is necessary but not sufficient for potential. Many high performers lack the aspiration, agility or engagement for bigger roles, while some high potentials are new in role. A good method assesses potential directly.

bank.question: Sundar's plant head retires in eight months. The best internal candidate is rated 'ready in 1-2 years'. Which combination of actions best manages the risk?
options: Promote the candidate now, since 'ready in 1-2 years' is close enough and she will learn quickly once in the role
Do nothing until the retirement date, then advertise externally
Name an interim (emergency) successor, accelerate the candidate's development, and keep an external option open
Ask the retiring head to postpone retirement indefinitely
bank.explanation: With no ready-now successor, the plan needs interim cover, accelerated development and a fallback. Promoting someone not yet ready raises failure risk, waiting leaves no lead time, and an indefinite delay is not a plan.

bank.question: Zoya scores key-person risk as likelihood × impact (each 1-5). The trade marketing head scores likelihood 4 and impact 5. The payroll officer scores likelihood 5 and impact 2. The finance controller scores likelihood 2 and impact 5. Which should be the first priority?
options: The payroll officer, because the likelihood of loss is highest
The finance controller, because impact matters more than likelihood
All three equally, because each has at least one score of 5
The trade marketing head, with a score of 20
bank.explanation: Scores are 4 × 5 = 20, 5 × 2 = 10 and 2 × 5 = 10. The trade marketing head has the highest combined risk. Looking at one dimension alone ignores the other.

bank.question: Much of Tariq's value lies in judgement: how he reads the boiler's sounds, which inspector cares about which records, and how to calm the halal certifier. What is the most effective way to transfer this knowledge?
options: Have the successor shadow him and then lead while he observes, with personal introductions to key contacts
Ask Tariq to write a detailed manual covering every procedure, contact and lesson before his last working day
Record a video interview with Tariq on his last day
Give the successor access to Tariq's email archive
bank.explanation: This is tacit knowledge, learned through experience and relationships, so it transfers best through shadowing, reverse shadowing and introductions. Manuals, videos and archives capture explicit knowledge but miss judgement and relationships.

bank.question: A group has 20 critical roles. Nine have at least one ready-now successor, 4 have only successors ready in 1-2 years, and 7 have none. What are its ready-now coverage and its share of critical roles with no successor?
options: 65% ready-now coverage; 35% with no successor
45% ready-now coverage; 35% with no successor
45% ready-now coverage; 55% with no successor
65% ready-now coverage; 20% with no successor
bank.explanation: Ready-now coverage = 9 ÷ 20 = 45%. Roles with no successor = 7 ÷ 20 = 35%. The 65% figure (13 ÷ 20) includes successors who are not yet ready.

bank.question: A telecom company is merging its regional structure and expects many senior roles to change shape within two years. Leaders want to know who will lead the new organisation. What should HR recommend?
options: Create a one-to-one replacement chart naming a successor for every current senior role in the existing structure
Freeze all development until the new structure is announced
Rely entirely on external hiring once the new roles are known
Develop talent pools for broad leadership capabilities rather than one named replacement per current role
bank.explanation: When roles are changing, pools developed for broad capabilities give flexibility. Replacement charts assume today's roles will persist, freezing development wastes two years, and external-only hiring is slow and costly.

bank.question: Noor Valley's best maintenance engineer was promoted to manage 25 technicians. Six months later his team's engagement has fallen, he spends evenings fixing machines himself, and he says he is unhappy. What should the company have offered him?
options: A specialist career track with senior technical roles and recognition
A larger team so that he could delegate more
A full management development course in the months before the promotion
A salary increase without any change in role
bank.explanation: He wanted growth, not people management. A dual ladder would have let him progress as a technical specialist. A course or a larger team does not change his aspiration, and a pay rise alone does not address growth.

bank.question: After a talent review, a manager tells an employee: 'You are a box 2, so you will never be promoted.' What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing is wrong: employees have a right to know their exact box and what it means for any future promotion here
The manager should have shown the whole grid with everyone's names
The 9-box is a snapshot for development talks; using it as a fixed label demotivates and ignores that potential changes
Box numbers should be shared only in writing, by HR
bank.explanation: The 9-box is a discussion tool reviewed regularly, and potential can change. Turning it into a fixed label damages motivation. Conversations should focus on development and opportunity, not boxes or guaranteed outcomes.

bank.question: Tariq agrees to a PKR 1.8m retention bonus to stay until July and transfer his knowledge. How should the bonus be structured to best protect Noor Valley?
options: Pay it all upfront to show trust and goodwill
Pay it in instalments tied to transfer milestones: procedures documented, Hina leading, key contacts handed over
Pay it all as one lump sum on his final working day, regardless of how much knowledge has been transferred by then
Pay it only if the plant receives no audit finding of any kind during the three years after Tariq's retirement
bank.explanation: Linking payments to knowledge-transfer milestones rewards what the company actually needs. Upfront payment removes the incentive, a lump sum on the last day rewards only staying, and a three-year condition he cannot control is unfair and unlikely to be accepted.

bank.question: Zoya estimates the full cost of losing the Lahore key-accounts manager at PKR 3.0m, and the chance that he leaves in the next year at 50% without action. A retention plan (a development assignment plus a PKR 0.6m retention bonus) is expected to cut that chance to 20%. Ignoring other benefits, what is the plan's expected net value?
options: PKR 0.3m positive
PKR 0.9m positive
PKR 2.4m positive
PKR 0.3m negative
bank.explanation: Expected loss without action = 50% × 3.0m = PKR 1.5m. With the plan = 20% × 3.0m = PKR 0.6m. Risk reduction = PKR 0.9m, minus the PKR 0.6m bonus = PKR 0.3m net positive. Forgetting the bonus cost gives PKR 0.9m.

bank.question: Which combination of signals points to the highest flight risk for a valued area manager?
options: Takes all her annual leave, recently married, and asked about the gratuity policy
Recently passed over for promotion, a new manager she does not know, and a compa-ratio of 0.82
Joined two months ago, attends every training session, and has a compa-ratio of 1.05
Has worked late every evening this month to close the quarter, and has asked the IT team for a new laptop
bank.explanation: Promotion setbacks, a manager change and pay well below midpoint are recognised triggers for leaving. Taking leave, getting married or asking a policy question are not reliable signals, and relying on assumptions such as marriage is biased.

bank.question: A top performer resigns, citing a rival's 25% higher offer. In the exit conversation she says the real issue is that her manager takes credit for her work. Her manager wants to counteroffer 30%. What is the main risk?
options: Counteroffers are not allowed under Pakistani labour law once an employee has formally submitted a resignation
She will certainly accept and then stay for many years, because a 30% rise outweighs any concern about her manager
A higher salary would reduce her motivation
The counteroffer leaves the real push factor untouched and may create pay inequity, so she may still leave later
bank.explanation: Counteroffers address the pull (money) while the push (her manager's behaviour) remains, and they can create inequity with peers. They are not illegal, and there is no guarantee she will stay.

bank.question: A Karachi call centre had an average headcount of 150 last quarter, and 9 agents left during that quarter. Roughly what is the annualised attrition rate?
bank.explanation: Quarterly attrition = 9 ÷ 150 = 6%. Annualised ≈ 6% × 4 = 24%, assuming no strong seasonal pattern. Reporting 6% as the annual rate understates the problem fourfold.

bank.question: An engineer earns PKR 210,000 a month. His grade's range is PKR 160,000 minimum, PKR 200,000 midpoint and PKR 240,000 maximum. What are his compa-ratio and range penetration?
options: Compa-ratio 1.05; range penetration 62.5%
Compa-ratio 0.95; range penetration 62.5%
Compa-ratio 1.05; range penetration 87.5%
Compa-ratio 1.31; range penetration 50%
bank.explanation: Compa-ratio = 210 ÷ 200 = 1.05. Range penetration = (210 − 160) ÷ (240 − 160) = 50 ÷ 80 = 62.5%. Dividing salary by the minimum gives 1.31, a different and wrong measure.

bank.question: A Lahore office's survey shows 40% promoters, 15% passives and 45% detractors. The site head says, 'With 55% scoring 7 or above, our eNPS is positive.' What is the actual eNPS?
bank.explanation: eNPS = % promoters − % detractors = 40 − 45 = −5. Passives (7-8) are excluded, so counting everyone at 7 and above does not give eNPS.

bank.question: Women TSOs leave at twice the rate of men. Exit interviews cite late-evening market visits without transport and a complaint about a supervisor that was never investigated. Which response best addresses the cause?
options: Stop hiring women into field sales, since attrition is higher
Run a resilience workshop for women TSOs
Add a special retention bonus for women TSOs who complete a full year, paid on the anniversary of their joining
Reschedule visits before dark with transport, and refer the complaint to the harassment inquiry committee
bank.explanation: The data points to systemic causes (unsafe scheduling and an unhandled complaint), which must be fixed. Excluding women is discriminatory, and a workshop or bonus places the burden on women without changing the system.

bank.question: A manager asks Zoya for engagement survey results for his team of three, 'to see who is unhappy'. What should Zoya do?
options: Send him the results with all names and employee numbers removed, so that the survey stays technically anonymous
Send the results, since the manager owns the team's data
Decline to report results for a group that small and offer them combined at a level that protects anonymity
Ask the three team members to tell their manager their scores directly
bank.explanation: With three people, results can easily be linked to individuals even without names, breaking the promise of confidentiality. Firms use minimum group sizes (often 5 to 10). Pressuring staff to disclose scores is worse.

bank.question: Zoya notices that TSOs who attended the optional leadership programme have half the attrition of those who did not. Bilal wants to tell the board, 'The programme halves attrition.' What is the main flaw?
options: The difference is too large to be believable
Attrition cannot be linked to training under any circumstances
The people who chose to attend may already have been more engaged, so the link may not be causal
Leadership programmes only ever affect Kirkpatrick Level 1 reactions, so they cannot have any effect on retention
bank.explanation: Volunteers often differ from non-volunteers (for example, they are more engaged), which is selection bias. Correlation is a clue, not proof of cause; a comparison of similar groups would be needed. Training can affect retention, so the other options overstate.

bank.question: Farzana has ten minutes with the board. Which set of measures best tells the talent story in business terms?
options: Number of training hours delivered, HR policies updated, job ads posted and recruitment events attended across Pakistan
Total headcount, number of HR staff and number of employee birthdays celebrated
Survey response rate, the number of exit interviews held during the year, and canteen and transport satisfaction scores
Regrettable attrition and its PKR cost, quality of hire, ready-now coverage of critical roles, and training ROI
bank.explanation: Boards act on measures that link people to business risk and value: losses of people you wanted to keep and their cost, whether hiring produces performers, readiness for critical roles, and returns on learning spend. The other sets measure activity, not impact.
